channel.description: Recent content in Api on Best of AI

item.title: Amazon SageMaker
item.description: SageMaker started as a way to run machine learning on AWS without managing servers. Data scientists use notebooks to prepare data and write code, then train models on managed compute that scales up as needed. Once a model is trained, SageMaker can deploy it behind an endpoint, monitor its performance, and handle versioning, which turns a notebook experiment into a production service. It supports popular frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow.

item.title: Apify
item.description: Apify turns the web into a source of structured data. A marketplace called Apify Store offers thousands of Actors, which are cloud programs that scrape or automate specific websites and tasks: extracting listings from Google Maps, posts from social networks, product details from e-commerce sites, or contact information from pages. You configure an Actor, run it in the cloud, and receive results as JSON, CSV, or through an API, without managing servers or proxies.

item.title: Builder.io
item.description:
Builder.io bridges developers and non-developers. Engineers integrate it into a website built with React, Vue, Next.js, or other frameworks, registering their components, and marketers and designers then assemble and edit pages visually using those components without waiting for a code release. That reduces bottlenecks for landing pages, campaigns, and content, while code stays under developers’ control.

AI has become central. Visual Copilot converts Figma designs into code in a chosen framework and styling approach, using the team’s own components where possible, which cuts down on the tedious work of translating designs. Newer offerings let teams describe features and have an AI agent build and update applications. A headless CMS manages structured content, and personalization and A/B testing features help optimize pages.

item.title: Codacy
item.description:
Codacy connects to repositories on GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket and analyzes code as it changes. It runs static analysis across many languages, checks for style problems, bugs, security issues, and complexity, and posts results as comments on pull requests. Teams can set quality gates that block merges when code does not meet agreed standards.

Dashboards show trends over time, including code coverage, duplication, and issue counts per repository, which helps engineering leads see whether quality is improving. Security features scan dependencies and secrets, and recent AI features suggest fixes and help review code produced by AI assistants. It integrates with CI systems and IDEs.

item.title: Crusoe
item.description:
Crusoe started with a particular idea: use natural gas that would otherwise be burned off at oil wells to power computers. That energy-first approach became a business in cloud computing and then in AI infrastructure, as demand for GPUs rose. Today it builds and operates data centers designed for high-density AI workloads.

Its cloud offers GPU instances, managed Kubernetes and Slurm, and managed inference services for running models, aimed at AI labs and companies that need large amounts of compute. The company emphasizes cleaner energy sources and large campuses for training clusters, working with chip makers and partners to deploy the latest hardware.

item.title: Daytona
item.description:
Daytona offers sandboxes for running code safely. AI agents that write and execute code need a place where mistakes or malicious instructions cannot harm real systems, and Daytona spins up an isolated environment on demand, runs the code, returns the results, and discards the sandbox. Fast startup keeps agent loops responsive.

The company started with standardized development environments that teams could create from a repository in one step. It turned toward infrastructure for AI agents, offering SDKs to create sandboxes, run commands, work with files, and snapshot state. The open-source core can be self-hosted, and a managed cloud is available.

item.title: Firebase
item.description:
Firebase lets developers build apps without running their own servers. Its core services are Cloud Firestore and Realtime Database for storing and syncing data, Authentication for sign-in with email, phone, or social accounts, Cloud Storage for files, Hosting for websites, and Cloud Functions for server-side code. Analytics, Crashlytics, and Cloud Messaging for push notifications round out the app lifecycle tools, and SDKs support iOS, Android, web, Flutter, and Unity.

AI has become part of the platform. Gemini in Firebase helps developers write code, debug, and understand their projects, and Firebase AI Logic gives apps a secure way to call Gemini and other models directly from the client. Genkit is an open-source framework for building AI features and agents, and Firebase Studio provides a browser-based environment for prototyping apps with AI assistance.

item.title: GPT4All
item.description:
GPT4All brings language models to personal computers. After installing the app on Windows, macOS, or Linux, you choose a model from a built-in list, download it, and chat without an internet connection. Everything runs on your own CPU or GPU, so your prompts and files do not go to a remote server.

A feature called LocalDocs lets you point the app at folders of your files so the model can answer questions about them using retrieval, which makes it useful as a private research or note assistant. The project is open source and also provides libraries and bindings for developers who want to integrate local models into their own software.

item.title: Gradio
item.description: Gradio makes it easy to show a model to other people. With a few lines of Python, you wrap a function, such as one that takes an image and returns a caption, and Gradio produces a web interface with the right input and output components: text boxes, image uploaders, audio recorders, sliders, and more. Running the script gives you a local web app, and a share option creates a temporary public link, which is handy for demos and feedback.

item.title: Heroku
item.description:
Heroku popularized the idea that deploying an app should be easy. A developer pushes code to a Git repository, and Heroku builds it, runs it in lightweight containers called dynos, and handles routing, scaling, and logs. Add-ons provide databases, caching, monitoring, and other services with a few clicks, so a small team can run a production app without managing servers. Many Ruby, Python, Node, and Java apps started there.

Heroku has been adding AI capabilities for developers. Managed inference lets apps call hosted models through the platform, and agent features help build and run AI-powered applications alongside the regular app and database, with the aim of keeping the developer experience simple. Heroku Postgres remains a central product, with pgvector support for embeddings.

item.title: LiveKit
item.description:
LiveKit started as an open-source WebRTC platform that handles the hard parts of real-time communication: routing audio and video between many participants, scaling to large rooms, and working across web and mobile. Developers use its SDKs to build video conferencing, livestreaming, telehealth, and interactive broadcast features, and can run it on their own servers or use the hosted LiveKit Cloud.

The company became prominent in voice AI. The Agents framework lets developers build agents that listen, think with a language model, and speak back, with low latency, handling details such as turn-taking and interruptions. It supports telephony so agents can answer phone calls, plus plugins for speech recognition, language, and voice providers. LiveKit powers voice features in well-known AI products, which helped establish it as a standard for real-time AI.

item.title: Moderne
item.description:
Moderne makes large-scale code change practical. OpenRewrite is an open-source refactoring engine that applies automated recipes to code, such as upgrading Java versions or replacing a deprecated API. Moderne indexes an organization’s repositories and runs recipes across all of them, producing pull requests.

That addresses the problem of maintaining hundreds of services. Instead of each team doing the same migration by hand, a platform team can run a recipe once and review the results. Search and analysis tools find where patterns occur, and AI assists in creating recipes and handling changes that rules cannot.

item.title: MongoDB Atlas
item.description:
MongoDB stores data as flexible JSON-like documents instead of rows and columns, which suits applications whose data shape changes often. Atlas runs it as a managed service: it handles provisioning, backups, scaling, and security, and works across the major clouds. Developers connect with drivers for most languages, and features like replication and sharding support high availability and large datasets. A free tier allows small projects and learning.

For AI, Atlas offers vector search alongside the regular database, so applications can store embeddings and run similarity queries without moving data to a separate vector database. This supports retrieval-augmented generation, recommendations, and semantic search. MongoDB has also acquired a company that builds embedding and reranking models, and integrates with common AI frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex. Full-text search, time-series, and analytics features sit in the same platform.

item.title: NVIDIA CUDA
item.description: CUDA is the software layer that lets programmers use an NVIDIA graphics processor for things other than graphics. You write functions called kernels, usually in C++ or Python, that run across thousands of GPU threads at once, which suits workloads built from large amounts of parallel math. Scientific simulation, video processing, and above all neural networks fit that description, so CUDA became the foundation for modern AI training and inference.

item.title: Redis
item.description: Redis stores data in memory, which makes reading and writing it extremely fast. Developers use it as a cache that sits in front of a slower database, as a session store for logged-in users, as a message queue, and for leaderboards, rate limiting, and counters. Its data types, such as lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, and streams, make these patterns easy to build with simple commands. It’s one of the most widely deployed pieces of infrastructure on the web.

item.title: SonarQube
item.description:
SonarQube analyzes source code without running it. It checks for bugs, security vulnerabilities, hardcoded secrets, code smells, duplication, and test coverage, and reports issues in a dashboard and in pull requests. Teams define quality gates, such as no new critical bugs, which can block a merge when code does not meet the standard, so problems are caught early in development.

It integrates with CI/CD systems like GitHub Actions, GitLab, Jenkins, and Azure DevOps, and with IDEs through SonarLint, which highlights issues as you type. AI features include CodeFix, which suggests changes for issues it finds, and capabilities designed to check AI-generated code, an area of growing concern as more code is written by assistants. It supports a large number of languages and frameworks.

item.title: Temporal
item.description:
Temporal addresses a hard part of building reliable software: making long-running, multi-step processes survive failures. Developers write workflows in an ordinary programming language such as Go, Java, Python, or TypeScript, and Temporal records each step and its state, so if a server crashes or a network call fails, the workflow continues from where it stopped without losing progress. Retries, timeouts, and timers are built in.

That makes it suitable for processes that take minutes to months, such as payment flows, order fulfillment, customer onboarding, infrastructure provisioning, and data processing. Increasingly, teams use it to orchestrate AI agents, where tasks call models and tools over long durations and need reliability and observability. Temporal Cloud provides a managed service, and the open-source server can be self-hosted.

item.title: Visual Studio Code
item.description: Visual Studio Code, usually called VS Code, is the most widely used code editor among developers. It is light enough to open quickly yet has what most people need: syntax highlighting, a debugger, integrated terminal, Git support, and a huge extension marketplace that adds languages, linters, themes, and tools. The core is open source, and it runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux. It also has a browser version, and remote development features let you work inside containers, over SSH, or in cloud environments.

item.title: Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic
item.description: Nova 2.5 Sonic reached general availability on October 5, 2026. It runs real-time voice agents with better tool-calling and lower latency than the previous version.

item.title: Canva Craft
item.description: Canva Craft is a design-focused image model that plans the composition and returns editable outputs up to 2K. It is available in Canva and through a public API.

item.title: Claude Haiku 5.5
item.description: Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7, 2026, for high-volume, cost-sensitive work. It has an adjustable effort setting and is available on the Claude Platform and through cloud providers.

item.title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Cyber
item.description: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Cyber is a cybersecurity-focused variant of V4.1 Flash, released October 29, 2026.

item.title: Doubao-Seedance-1.0-pro-fast
item.description: Doubao-Seedance-1.0-pro-fast is a faster, cheaper version of Seedance 1.0 Pro, up to about 3x quicker, with multi-shot generation. It runs on Volcano Ark.

item.title: FLUX 3 Max
item.description: FLUX 3 Max is a higher-tier model in Black Forest Labs’ FLUX 3 line, listed by LLM Gateway as released October 15, 2026.

item.title: Gemini Robotics ER 2
item.description: Gemini Robotics ER 2 is a robotics reasoning model that entered public preview on Google Cloud on October 27, 2026, with enterprise tooling.

item.title: GPT-6.1 Terra
item.description: GPT-6.1 Terra is the fast, efficient model in OpenAI’s GPT-6 family, with visual reasoning and computer use. OpenAI lists its standard API prices at 50% below GPT-5.6 Terra.

item.title: Grok Voice 3.0
item.description: Grok Voice 3.0 is xAI’s speech-to-speech model for the Voice Agent API. The grok-voice-latest alias now points to it.

item.title: MAI-Voice-2.1
item.description: Microsoft released MAI-Voice-2.1 and a low-latency MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash on October 1, 2026, alongside MAI-Transcribe-2-Streaming, which transcribes live speech in 60 languages with partial results in just over 100 ms.

item.title: Mercury 3
item.description: Mercury 3 is a diffusion-based language model from Inception Labs with a 1M-token context window.

item.title: MiMo V2.6 Flash
item.description: MiMo V2.6 Flash is the lower-cost companion to Xiaomi’s MiMo V2.6 Pro, listed on API aggregators in October 2026 with a 128K context window. The exact release date is unconfirmed.

item.title: Muse Wonder
item.description: Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are agent models that use Active Memory and Active Focus for long tasks. They are available through the Meta Model API and Muse Code.

item.title: Nano Banana 2.1
item.description: Nano Banana 2.1 is an image generation and editing model in the Gemini 3 family, taking text and images in and returning images and text. It is available in Gemini, AI Studio, Ads, Flow, and other Google products.

item.title: Step 5 Preview
item.description: StepFun’s Step 5 Preview appeared on API aggregators in October 2026 with a 128K context window. StepFun has not published much detail, and the exact release date is unconfirmed.

item.title: Voxtral 3
item.description: Voxtral 3 covers both speech-to-text and text-to-speech and comes with a voice-agent SDK. Mistral hosts the API in the EU and also offers self-deployment.

item.title: Claude Opus 5.5
item.description: Anthropic released Claude Opus 5.5 on September 22, 2026, keeping the 1 million token context window of Claude Opus 5 while matching Claude Fable 5.1 on most of Anthropic’s benchmark suite. The main change is cost: Anthropic says Opus 5.5 runs roughly 40% cheaper than Opus 5 on typical workloads, making it a straight upgrade for teams already on the Opus tier rather than a separate product line.

item.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5
item.description: Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5 on September 28, 2026, a week after Claude Opus 5.5. Anthropic says it generates output more than 30% faster than Claude Sonnet 5 while keeping the same API pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached-input reads at $0.20. The context window stays at 1 million tokens.

item.title: Eleven v4
item.description: ElevenLabs launched Eleven v4 on September 28, 2026, improving expressiveness and voice cloning (down to a 10-second sample) across more than 90 languages. Eleven v4 Turbo is the same model tuned for real-time use, running at roughly 100 milliseconds of median latency. Eleven v4 ranked first on the Artificial Analysis Provider Voice Arena leaderboard for September 2026, with about 75% of listeners preferring it over five rival services in blind tests.

item.title: GLM-5.3-FlashX
item.description: Z.ai (Zhipu AI) released GLM-5.3-FlashX on September 18, 2026, carrying over GLM-5.3-Flash’s 320-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts design with 18 billion active parameters per token, native multimodality, and hybrid sparse-plus-linear attention. The FlashX variant is tuned for serving speed, targeting throughput up to 200 tokens per second, while keeping the same 1 million token context window.

item.title: GPT-6 Luna
item.description: OpenAI released GPT-6 Luna on September 22, 2026, as the budget sibling to GPT-6 Sol. It shares Sol’s 1.05 million token context window and 128,000 token output limit but costs far less to run, at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, making it OpenAI’s pick for high-volume tasks like classification, summarization, and routine chat where the heavier reasoning of GPT-6 Astra or Sol isn’t needed.

item.title: GPT-6 Sol
item.description: OpenAI released GPT-6 Sol on September 22, 2026, alongside the cheaper GPT-6 Luna, positioning both below the earlier GPT-6 Astra flagship in the GPT-6 lineup. Sol reads up to 1.05 million tokens of context and writes up to 128,000 tokens of output, aimed at coding and agentic tasks rather than Astra’s recurrent-depth reasoning. API pricing runs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with a $0.20 rate for cached input.

item.title: Grok 4.7
item.description: xAI released Grok 4.7 on September 21, 2026, alongside Grok Build, a terminal-native coding agent built around it. The model keeps the same per-token pricing as Grok 4.6 and offers a 500,000 token context window. Grok 5 is still in training at xAI with no committed release date, making 4.7 an interim update aimed mostly at coding and knowledge-work tasks.

item.title: Qwen-Audio-3.1-Realtime
item.description: Alibaba released Qwen-Audio-3.1-Realtime on September 28, 2026 as the flagship of a five-model Qwen-Audio-3.1 stack that also covers speech recognition and text-to-speech. It’s built for full-duplex voice agents, meaning it can listen and respond at the same time and decide mid-conversation when to speak versus when to call an external tool.

item.title: Qwen-Image-2.1
item.description: Alibaba open-sourced Qwen-Image-2.1 on September 20, 2026. The 7-billion-parameter model merges text-to-image generation and image editing into a single system, supports a real alpha channel for transparent output, and accepts up to 10 reference images per generation. Weights are available on Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license.

item.title: Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash
item.description: Alibaba released Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash in late September 2026 as a single model that accepts text, image, audio, and video input and responds in text, built for agentic and multimodal workloads. It carries a 1 million token context window and is available through Alibaba Cloud and as open weights on Hugging Face.

item.title: Xiaomi MiMo-V2.6-Pro
item.description: Xiaomi open-sourced the MiMo-V2.6 line on September 22, 2026, made up of MiMo-V2.6-Flash, the flagship MiMo-V2.6-Pro, and a faster inference variant called MiMo-V2.6-Pro-UltraSpeed. The release leans on reinforcement-learning gains from Xiaomi’s research team, and the company cites inference throughput above 150 tokens per second as one of the family’s selling points. MiMo-V2.6-Pro ships under the MIT license.

item.title: Claude Mythos 5.1
item.description: Claude Mythos 5.1 shares the same underlying model as Claude Fable 5.1, released the same day, but ships with the guardrails loosened for a narrow set of dual-use tasks: vulnerability discovery, red teaming, drug discovery, and biodefense screening. Anthropic isn’t putting it in the regular API lineup: access goes only to organizations vetted through its trusted-access programs, and pricing matches Fable 5.1 at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens.

item.title: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
item.description:
DeepSeek shipped V4.1-Flash on September 10, 2026, a 552-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with native vision support and a 1,048,576 token context window that extends to 393,216 tokens of output. Pricing runs on a peak/off-peak split: off-peak rates are $0.003 per million input tokens on a cache hit, $0.15 on a cache miss, and $0.60 per million output tokens, with peak-hour rates (weekday mornings UTC) exactly double.

The tiered pricing is DeepSeek leaning into its usual playbook: undercut Western API pricing hard during low-demand windows to pull in batch and non-latency-sensitive workloads, while still charging enough at peak to manage capacity.

item.title: Fugu Max
item.description: Fugu Max, released by Sakana AI on September 11, 2026 alongside its flagship sibling Fugu Ultra v2, isn’t a foundation model in the usual sense. It’s a routing model trained to farm tasks out across a fixed pool of open-weight and specialized models, including NVIDIA’s Nemotron family, and to call instances of itself recursively. Sakana prices it at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens, which the company claims is 40 to 60 percent cheaper on output than Sonnet 5, GPT-5.6 Terra, and Kimi K3.

item.title: Fugu Ultra v2
item.description: Fugu Ultra v2 is Sakana AI’s flagship orchestration model, released September 11, 2026 at $5 per million input tokens and $30 per million output tokens for standard context lengths. Rather than being trained as one network, it routes and recombines a pool of open-weight and specialized models under a 1 million token context window. On Chartography, Sakana’s visual-reasoning and data-interpretation benchmark, it scored 48.3 against 27.3 for Anthropic’s Opus 5 and 29.5 for Fable 5.

item.title: Gemini 3.8 Flash
item.description:
Google pushed out Gemini 3.8 Flash on September 2, 2026, keeping the same 1,048,576 token context window and 65,536 token output ceiling as 3.7 Flash while posting solid gains on software engineering, agentic, and multi-step reasoning benchmarks. Introductory pricing holds at $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens through the end of 2026, after which it doubles to $1.50 and $7.50.

Alongside it, Google released Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, a locked-down variant tuned for vulnerability discovery and patching, available only to vetted defenders through the new Fairwind Program rather than the general API.

item.title: Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber
item.description: Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber is Google’s dedicated security model, released alongside the general-purpose 3.8 Flash on September 2, 2026, and gated behind the new Fairwind Program rather than sold as a standard API product. Google says it clears 70 percent-plus on internal vulnerability-discovery tests across 20 languages, scores 47.2 percent pass@1 on CWE-Bench, and delivers 2.6 times more correct patches to Chrome vulnerabilities than leading commercial models in the company’s own testing.

item.title: Gemini 3.8 Live
item.description: Google released Gemini 3.8 Live on September 15, 2026, alongside a reasoning-heavier sibling called Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking. Both run over a WebSocket connection through the Gemini Live API, take audio, video, images, and text as input, and reply in audio, understanding and speaking 97 languages with the ability to switch languages mid-conversation. Pricing runs $0.005 per minute of audio input and $0.018 per minute of audio output, which works out to roughly $1.38 for an hour of conversation.

item.title: Kimi K2.8 Preview
item.description: Moonshot AI rolled out Kimi K2.8 Preview on September 11, 2026, slotting it between the open-weight Kimi K2.7 Code and flagship Kimi K3. It landed inside Kimi Code and Kimi Work the same day with no configuration changes needed, added image and video input on top of text, and bumped every membership tier’s context window from 262,144 to 1 million tokens. Adjustable thinking effort (low, high, or max) now matches the K3 series, with max as the default.

item.title: Mercury 2.5 Preview
item.description: Inception Labs released Mercury 2.5 Preview on August 31, 2026, the latest in its Mercury line of diffusion language models, a design that generates and refines multiple tokens in parallel rather than one at a time. Inception says the approach pushes throughput to 1,107 tokens per second on standard GPUs. Inception puts the intelligence gain over Mercury 2 at around 40 percent, in range with cost-optimized models like Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and Claude Haiku 4.5.

item.title: Claude Fable 5.1
item.description: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1 on September 1, 2026, alongside Mythos 5.1, a restricted-access version of the same underlying model available to vetted cybersecurity and life-sciences organizations that need capabilities the public release keeps guarded. Fable 5.1 keeps the same $10 per million input and $50 per million output token pricing as Fable 5, but cuts prompt-cache reads from $1.00 to $0.25 per million tokens, a change Anthropic says lowers effective cost by around 25 percent for typical workloads and as much as 45 percent for heavily agentic ones that lean on cached context. Anthropic reported 52.6 percent on Terminal-Bench-Science as one of the headline benchmark gains over the original Fable 5.

item.title: GPT-6 Astra
item.description: OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra on September 3, 2026, its most capable model yet and the first to use what the company calls recurrent depth, a looped reasoning technique that lets the model revisit and refine its read of a problem multiple times rather than reasoning in a single forward pass. Pricing runs $10 per million input tokens, $1 for cached input, $12.50 for cache writes, and $50 per million output tokens, with a 1.05 million token context window and up to 128,000 tokens of output. The approach has drawn scrutiny from outside safety researchers, including groups at Redwood Research, who note that recurrent depth makes the model’s chain of thought harder for outside observers to monitor compared with earlier step-by-step reasoning models.

item.title: Muse Spark 1.3
item.description: Meta shipped Muse Spark 1.3 on September 2, 2026, its biggest coding and agentic jump yet and, according to AI chief Alexandr Wang, a model that closes much of the gap with frontier releases like GPT-5.6. It cuts token usage by 25 percent and tool calls by 20 percent on comparable tasks, and holds the same $1.25 per million input and $4.25 per million output token pricing as its predecessor, plus a contributor tier at a steep discount for developers who let Meta train on their prompts and completions. Access starts through Muse Code and the Meta API, with a “max reasoning” variant still going through safety testing before release, and a rollout to Meta AI, Instagram, and Facebook planned to follow.

item.title: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp
item.description: DeepSeek released DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp on August 21, 2026 as an experimental image-input variant of DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the sparse mixture-of-experts model with 284 billion total parameters and 13 billion active per token. It matches the text-only V4-Flash on agentic and reasoning tasks while adding image understanding, aimed at document and chart reading, visual question answering, and agent workflows that mix text and images. Images can be passed as inline base64 data, URLs, or through DeepSeek’s Files API, and the model tokenizes each image at 384 tokens, well below what GPT and Claude models typically use per image.

item.title: GLM-5.2 Turbo
item.description: Zhipu AI released GLM-5.2 Turbo on August 17, 2026 as a faster sibling to GLM-5.2, built specifically for agent-driven workloads rather than general chat or one-off queries. It carries a smaller context window than the base model, about 200,000 tokens versus GLM-5.2’s full 1-million-token capacity, in exchange for lower latency on the long execution chains typical of coding agents and automation tools. Zhipu says it improved complex instruction decomposition and tool use, along with stability across scheduled and persistent tasks that run for extended periods without human supervision.

item.title: GPT-5.6 Cyber
item.description: OpenAI released GPT-5.6 Cyber on August 10, 2026, built on top of GPT-5.6 Sol and trained specifically to help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities faster than attackers can exploit them. It sits behind Daybreak Red, a new, more restricted tier of OpenAI’s Daybreak cyber defense program that requires separate vetting beyond the general Daybreak Blue access most approved security teams get. Compared with the base GPT-5.6 Sol model, GPT-5.6 Cyber has far fewer refusals on dual-use security requests, completing 95 percent of advanced tasks on OpenAI’s internal cybersecurity evaluation versus 1.5 percent for the general model.

item.title: Grok 4.6
item.description: xAI released Grok 4.6 on August 12, 2026, extending Grok 4.5’s coding focus toward longer-running agent sessions and more demanding interactive and visual tasks. The model carries a 500,000-token context window, accepts text and image input, and exposes configurable reasoning effort levels from low to xhigh so developers can trade off latency against depth on a given request. xAI priced it at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens for prompts under 200,000 tokens, with rates roughly doubling once a request crosses that threshold.

item.title: Qwen-Image-3.0
item.description: Alibaba announced Qwen-Image-3.0 on July 21, 2026 with invite-only access, then opened it fully on August 5. The third generation of Alibaba’s image line, it is built around accepting much longer instructions than its predecessor, up to roughly 4,500 tokens versus about 1,000 for Qwen-Image 2.0, so it can compose dense, information-heavy layouts like infographics, slide decks, and UI mockups in a single pass. It also renders small text accurately down to about 10 pixels across a dozen languages, an area where earlier image models tended to produce garbled or illegible characters.

item.title: DeepSeek Harness
item.description:
DeepSeek Harness is a framework for running agents that work on code. It provides the loop that lets a model plan, call tools, read and edit files, run shell commands, and report back, similar in purpose to terminal agents from other labs. Its notable design choice is that nearly every part is a plugin: the model adapter, tool registry, session log, and the agent loop itself can be replaced.

It includes presets for common setups, such as a standard coding agent with filesystem and shell tools, web search, subagents, and a planning mode, and a mode for building custom presets. Sandboxing uses the operating system’s own mechanisms to limit what the agent can touch. Although DeepSeek made it, it can connect to models from other providers.

item.title: Gemini 3.7 Flash
item.description: Google shipped Gemini 3.7 Flash on August 13, 2026, just three weeks after 3.6 Flash, keeping the same 1,048,576 token input window and 65,536 token output ceiling while moving the knowledge cutoff to March 2026. Google credits the gains to developer feedback and algorithmic changes rather than a bigger model, and the benchmark jumps are large: DeepSWE v1.1 climbs from 49.0 to 65.3 percent, FrontierCode 1.1 Main goes from 34.4 to 43.6 percent, and Zapier’s AutomationBench nearly doubles from 17.0 to 30.4 percent. Input pricing is cut in half to $0.75 per million tokens as introductory pricing through the end of 2026.

item.title: FLUX 3
item.description: FLUX 3 is Black Forest Labs’ first model to train images, video, and audio together in a single architecture instead of stitching separate generators behind one interface. From a single prompt it can produce a still image or a combined video-and-audio clip up to 20 seconds long, and the same underlying approach, which the company calls Self-Flow, extends to robotic vision and action prediction. It launched July 23, 2026 in a limited release rather than a full public rollout, continuing FLUX’s role powering generative features inside tools like Adobe Photoshop and Picsart. Pricing and access remain narrower than the rest of the FLUX line at launch, with Black Forest Labs prioritizing existing API and platform partners before opening it more broadly.

item.title: Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber
item.description: Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber is a specialized variant Google fine-tuned for finding and fixing security vulnerabilities, released July 21, 2026 as part of the same drop that introduced Gemini 3.6 Flash and Flash-Lite. Rather than a general release, Google is running it as a limited access pilot restricted to governments and trusted partners, reflecting how sensitive vulnerability-discovery capabilities are treated differently from general-purpose coding models. Technical specs mirror the rest of the Gemini 3.5 Flash line, but pricing and broader availability have not been published since the model sits behind pilot-program approval rather than open self-serve API access.

item.title: Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite
item.description: Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite shipped July 21, 2026 alongside Gemini 3.6 Flash as the cheapest model in the current Gemini lineup, aimed at teams running high-volume, latency-sensitive workloads like classification and bulk summarization rather than complex reasoning. It shares the 1,048,576 token context window with its larger Flash siblings and takes text, image, audio, and video input. Pricing runs $0.30 per million input tokens and $2.50 per million output tokens, with a flat 50 percent discount in batch mode for non-real-time jobs. Google positions it as the entry point into the Gemini 3.5 family for developers who need to process large volumes of requests cheaply and can route only the harder cases up to Flash or Pro.

item.title: Gemini 3.6 Flash
item.description: Gemini 3.6 Flash replaced Gemini 3.5 Flash as Google’s default workhorse model on July 21, 2026, part of a three-model July drop that also included Flash-Lite and a restricted Flash Cyber variant, with Gemini 3.5 Pro still not shipped. It keeps the 1,048,576 token context window and 65,536 token output ceiling, moves the knowledge cutoff to March 2026, and uses about 17 percent fewer output tokens than its predecessor while scoring higher on coding, long-context, and computer-use benchmarks, including a jump from 37 to 49 percent on DeepSWE. Output pricing dropped from $9.00 to $7.50 per million tokens, with input still at $1.50 per million and cached input at $0.15 per million. Independent evaluations are more mixed than Google’s own numbers suggest: the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index scores it even with 3.5 Flash, and community coding tests put it behind GPT-5.6 Luna, Grok 4.5, and Kimi K3 on several tasks.

item.title: Muse Spark 1.2
item.description: Muse Spark 1.2 is a coding-focused point release of Muse Spark 1.1 rather than a new base model, shipped August 5, 2026 alongside Muse Code, Meta’s first terminal coding agent. It keeps the 1,048,576 token context window and roughly 131,072 max output tokens from 1.1, and was co-trained with the new agent using rejection-sampled harness trajectories plus a self-improvement loop. Meta reports a jump from 76.2 to 82.9 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and from 53.0 to 59.3 percent on DeepSWE v1.1 over the previous version. Standard API pricing holds at $1.25 per million input tokens and $4.25 per million output tokens, and Meta added a separate contributor tier at $0.10 input and $0.20 output in exchange for permission to train future models on submitted prompts and completions.

item.title: Qwen3.8-Max
item.description: Qwen3.8-Max is Alibaba’s largest and most capable model to date, previewed July 19, 2026 and officially launched August 3 with published specs and pricing. It’s a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 2.4 trillion total parameters and roughly 95 billion active per token, handles text, image, and video input across a 1 million token context window, and Alibaba has pitched it as trailing only Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 on its own benchmark comparisons. It ranked fifth in Text Arena and second in Vision Arena shortly after launch. The model is available now through Alibaba Cloud’s Model Studio and Qwen Chat, with open weights planned for release the following week, which would make it the largest model Alibaba has open-sourced at this scale.

item.title: Cloudflare Kitesurf
item.description:
Kitesurf rethinks the browser for software. Most automation tools control a full desktop browser, which is heavy and built around human use. Kitesurf is a lean browser written to run inside Cloudflare’s Workers platform, so an agent can open pages, read them, and click or type without the overhead of a complete Chrome instance.

It works with existing tools. Clients that use Puppeteer, Playwright, or the Model Context Protocol can connect to it through Cloudflare’s browser service with small changes. The design treats every page as untrusted and starts each session fresh, which suits agent security. Cloudflare says it uses less memory than Chromium in its tests.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.5
item.description: Claude Opus 4.5 is the Opus-tier model Anthropic released on November 24, 2025, and its headline change was price: input tokens dropped to $5 per million and output to $25 per million, a two-thirds cut from Opus 4.1’s $15/$75 rate. It scored 80.9 percent on SWE-bench Verified at launch, ahead of Gemini 3 Pro’s 76.2 percent and GPT-5.1 Codex Max’s 77.9 percent on the same benchmark, and Anthropic added an “effort” parameter that lets developers dial reasoning depth up or down per request. It kept the 200,000 token context window and image input support from earlier Opus releases, and shipped alongside a round of Claude Code updates aimed at longer autonomous coding sessions. Anthropic followed it with Opus 4.6 in February 2026 and Opus 4.7 in April, each holding the same $5/$25 pricing while pushing coding scores further.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.6
item.description: Claude Opus 4.6, released February 5, 2026, expanded the Opus line’s context window to 1 million tokens, up from the 200,000 tokens Opus 4.5 shipped with three months earlier. Anthropic held pricing steady at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens and focused the update on coding: the model plans more carefully before writing code, sustains agentic tasks over longer sessions, and catches more of its own mistakes during code review. It’s available across claude.ai, the Claude API, and the major cloud platforms, and it became the base Anthropic built the Sonnet 4.6 release on two weeks later.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.7
item.description: Claude Opus 4.7, released April 16, 2026, is a direct upgrade to Opus 4.6 aimed at the hardest software engineering tasks, the ones where earlier Opus models still stumbled on large, unfamiliar codebases. Pricing held at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, and it kept the 1 million token context window with up to 128,000 tokens of output. It shipped with a new tokenizer that produces up to 35 percent more tokens for the same input text, a tradeoff Anthropic made to improve accuracy on code-heavy prompts. It’s available through claude.ai, the API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry.

item.title: Claude Opus 5
item.description: Claude Opus 5 is Anthropic’s newest Opus-tier model, released July 24, 2026 at the same $5/$25 per million token pricing as Opus 4.8, half of what the larger Claude Fable 5 model charges for similar intelligence. It ships with a low, medium, and high effort toggle so developers can trade cost against reasoning depth on a per-request basis, plus a faster mode that doubles the price to $10/$50 in exchange for roughly 2.5 times the speed. On SWE-bench Pro it scored 79.2 percent, roughly double the agentic coding score Anthropic reported for the previous Opus generation, and it posted 43.3 percent on Frontier-Bench and 30.2 percent on ARC-AGI-3. It carries the 1 million token context window that has been standard across the Opus line since Opus 4.6, and it’s available on claude.ai, the API, and the major cloud platforms from launch.

item.title: Claude Sonnet 4.6
item.description: Claude Sonnet 4.6 shipped on February 17, 2026 and became the default model in claude.ai and Claude Cowork, Anthropic’s workspace product. It matches Opus 4.6’s 1 million token context window and 128,000 token output limit while pricing in at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, roughly a fifth of Opus 4.6’s rate. On SWE-bench Verified it scored 79.6 percent, within a few points of the Opus model despite the price gap, and it posted 59.1 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and 72.5 percent on OSWorld-Verified, benchmarks that test agentic terminal and computer-use tasks. Anthropic built in extended reasoning chains that can run up to 100 steps, aimed at developers who want Opus-level reliability without paying Opus prices.

item.title: Gemini 3 Flash
item.description: Gemini 3 Flash, released December 17, 2025, brought Gemini 3 Pro’s reasoning quality down to Flash-tier latency and cost. It carries a 1 million token input context window and handles multimodal input across text, image, audio, and video, with pricing starting at $0.50 per million input tokens and $3.00 per million output tokens. Google positioned it as the default model for the Gemini app and API workloads that don’t need Pro-level depth, and it remained the workhorse Flash tier until Gemini 3.5 Flash replaced it in May 2026.

item.title: Gemini 3.1 Pro
item.description: Gemini 3.1 Pro is Google’s generally available successor to Gemini 3 Pro, released February 19, 2026 with a 1 million token context window and up to 64,000 tokens of output across text, image, video, and audio. Google reports 80.6 percent on SWE-bench Verified, 94.3 percent on GPQA Diamond, and 77.1 percent on ARC-AGI-2, where it placed second behind OpenAI’s GPT-5.5. Pricing held at $2.00 per million input tokens and $12.00 per million output tokens for prompts under 200,000 tokens, doubling to $4.00/$18.00 beyond that threshold, with cached input available at $0.20 per million. It’s available through the Gemini app, Google AI Studio, Vertex AI, and the Gemini API, and it remained Google’s flagship model until Gemini 3.5 Pro’s rollout later in 2026.

item.title: Gemini 3.5 Flash
item.description: Gemini 3.5 Flash launched at Google I/O on May 20, 2026 and immediately replaced Gemini 3 Flash as the default model in the Gemini app, Google Search’s AI Mode, and the Gemini API. It handles a 1,048,576 token input window with up to 65,536 tokens of output across text, image, audio, and video, and Google says it runs about four times faster than other frontier models while beating Gemini 3.1 Pro on several coding and agentic benchmarks, including 76.2 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1. Pricing is $1.50 per million input tokens and $9.00 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens discounted 90 percent to $0.15 per million, and dynamic thinking is enabled by default rather than requiring a separate flag.

item.title: GPT-5 Pro
item.description: GPT-5 Pro is the highest-compute variant of GPT-5, released October 6, 2025 for tasks where accuracy matters more than speed or cost. It shares GPT-5’s 400,000 token context window with up to 272,000 tokens of output, and OpenAI prices it well above the standard model at $15 per million input tokens and $120 per million output tokens. It runs longer internal reasoning chains than default GPT-5, trading latency for higher accuracy on hard math, science, and coding problems, and it’s available through ChatGPT Pro and the API rather than the free or Plus tiers. OpenAI kept the same pattern with Pro variants of each GPT-5.x release that followed.

item.title: GPT-5.1
item.description: GPT-5.1 is OpenAI’s update to GPT-5, released November 13, 2025 with an emphasis on coding and agentic tasks. It carries the same 400,000 token context window as GPT-5, with up to 128,000 tokens of output, and API pricing held at $1.25 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input priced at $0.125 per million. The model exposes a reasoning-effort setting with none, low, medium, and high options, giving developers more control over how much internal deliberation a request gets than GPT-5’s automatic routing offered. OpenAI positioned it as a refinement rather than a new generation, shipped to close gaps competitors had opened up on coding benchmarks in the months since GPT-5’s August 2025 launch.

item.title: GPT-5.2
item.description: GPT-5.2 arrived December 11, 2025 in three variants: GPT-5.2 Instant for quick responses, GPT-5.2 Thinking for step-by-step reasoning, and GPT-5.2 Pro for the hardest problems. It kept the 400,000 token context window and 128,000 token output limit from the GPT-5.1 generation, and OpenAI priced the standard model at $1.75 per million input tokens and $14 per million output tokens, with a five-level reasoning effort setting from minimal to extra high. By mid-2026 OpenAI was steering users toward the newer GPT-5.6 line, but GPT-5.2 remains available in the API and ChatGPT’s legacy model picker.

item.title: GPT-5.4
item.description: GPT-5.4, released March 5, 2026, was the first general-purpose OpenAI model to ship with native computer-use capability, reaching 75 percent on the OSWorld benchmark for controlling a desktop environment directly. It expanded the context window to roughly 1 million tokens (922,000 input plus 128,000 output), added a five-level reasoning effort control, and introduced a tool-search mechanism that OpenAI says cuts token costs by 47 percent in workflows that call a lot of external tools. Standard API pricing is $2.50 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with a GPT-5.4 Pro tier at $30/$180 for maximum accuracy. OpenAI followed up on March 17 with GPT-5.4 Mini, priced at $0.75/$4.50 and available to free ChatGPT users, plus a developer-only GPT-5.4 Nano tier.

item.title: GPT-5.5
item.description: GPT-5.5, released April 23, 2026 with API access following the next day, pushed the context window to roughly 1 million tokens and lands meaningfully above GPT-5.4 on long-context recall, multi-step tool use, and code generation in large repositories, though it costs more per token. Standard pricing is $5 per million input tokens and $30 per million output tokens, with GPT-5.5 Pro available at $30/$180 for the hardest problems, and OpenAI offers batch and flex pricing at half the standard rate alongside a 2.5 times priority tier for latency-sensitive use. It topped the ARC-AGI-2 leaderboard at roughly 85 percent, the highest score any model had reached on that benchmark at the time, and OpenAI replaced it with GPT-5.6 less than three months later.

item.title: Grok 4.20
item.description: Grok 4.20 is xAI’s multi-agent model, with a beta launching February 17, 2026 and the dated release following on March 9. Its defining feature is a native four-agent system, internally named Grok, Harper, Benjamin, and Lucas, that reasons in parallel and debates internally before returning a single answer, which xAI says cut hallucinations by 65 percent compared to Grok 4.1. It runs on a roughly 3 trillion parameter mixture-of-experts backbone with a context window up to 2 million tokens, operates in separate reasoning and non-reasoning modes, and keeps the real-time X data integration xAI has used across the Grok line. API pricing is $1.25 per million input tokens, $0.20 for cached input, and $2.50 per million output tokens, well below the $2/$6 xAI charged for Grok 4.5 seven months earlier.

item.title: Amazon Nova 2 Pro
item.description: Amazon Nova 2 Pro is the first refresh of the Nova Pro tier since the original family launched at re:Invent 2024, and it’s exclusive to AWS Bedrock like the rest of the line. It moves the context window up to 500,000 tokens and adds video understanding alongside text and image, priced at $1.50 per million input tokens and $6.00 per million output tokens, a jump from the original Nova Pro that reflects the added capability.

item.title: Command A2
item.description:
Command A2 succeeds Command A as Cohere’s flagship model, keeping the same enterprise-first pitch: strong retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, and multilingual support over chasing chatbot benchmarks. It’s priced at $2.50 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, and it’s reachable through Cohere’s own API as well as AWS Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry, and Oracle Cloud, the same multi-cloud distribution Cohere has relied on since Command R.

Cohere continues to sell mainly to enterprises building internal search and document-QA systems rather than consumer-facing products, and Command A2’s improvements are aimed squarely at that audience: better grounding on retrieved documents and more reliable citation of sources, both areas where the company has staked its reputation against larger labs with flashier general-purpose models.

item.title: Mistral Large 4
item.description: Mistral Large 4 replaces Large 3 as Mistral AI’s proprietary flagship, roughly eight months after that model shipped in December 2025. It’s a 190 billion parameter dense model with a 256,000 token context window, priced at $2 per million input tokens and $8 per million output tokens through Mistral’s own La Plateforme as well as Azure AI Foundry and AWS Bedrock. Mistral says the gains over Large 3 are concentrated in coding and multi-step reasoning, an area where the company has been trying to close the gap with GPT-5.6 and Claude Sonnet 5 rather than compete on raw scale.

item.title: Qwen4-Max
item.description: Qwen4-Max is Alibaba’s top-tier proprietary model, sitting above the open-weight Qwen3 family the company keeps releasing on Hugging Face. Unlike those, Qwen4-Max is closed and only reachable through Alibaba Cloud’s API, Qwen Chat, or partner platforms, priced at $1.20 per million input tokens and $4.80 per million output tokens. It takes text and image input, carries a 1 million token context window, and Alibaba has been positioning it directly against GPT-5.6 and Gemini 3.5 Pro in its own benchmark comparisons.

item.title: Runway Gen-5
item.description:
Runway Gen-5 is the follow-up to Gen-4, extending maximum clip length and giving directors finer camera control: pans, tilts, and focus pulls specified as explicit parameters rather than left for the model to infer from a text prompt. Like its predecessors it takes text and image input and outputs video, available through Runway’s own app and API rather than as open weights.

Runway has kept pace with Google’s Veo and OpenAI’s Sora releases by shipping frequently and leaning into workflow features (multi-shot consistency, motion brushes, camera controls) that professional editors ask for, rather than only chasing raw fidelity. Gen-5 continues that pattern, with Runway pitching it primarily at studios and ad agencies already using Gen-4 in production pipelines rather than at hobbyist creators.

item.title: AMD ROCm
item.description:
ROCm is AMD’s answer to NVIDIA’s CUDA. It is a collection of software that lets programs use AMD graphics processors for general computing, including drivers, a compiler toolchain, math and communication libraries, and tools for debugging and profiling. Much of it is open source.

For AI work, the key piece is framework support. PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, and others run on ROCm, and inference tools like vLLM and many model libraries have AMD builds. Developers can port CUDA code using HIP, a programming layer that resembles CUDA, and large cloud and supercomputer deployments use AMD Instinct accelerators with ROCm.

item.title: Braintrust
item.description:
Braintrust helps teams treat AI quality like software quality. Developers log each model call and agent step, then build datasets of test cases from real traffic. Scorers, including programmatic checks and language model judges, rate outputs, so a change to a prompt or model can be tested before it ships.

The product combines several pieces. A playground lets teams compare prompts and models side by side, experiments track results over time, and online monitoring scores production traffic and raises alerts. A gateway can route calls to different model providers, and collaboration features let engineers and non-engineers review outputs.

item.title: Cloudflare AI Gateway
item.description:
AI Gateway is a proxy for calls to language models. A developer points their app’s requests at a Cloudflare URL instead of the provider’s, and the gateway forwards them while recording what happens. This gives a dashboard of requests, tokens, costs, and errors across providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

It adds control features. Caching returns stored answers for repeated requests to save money and time, rate limits protect budgets, and retries and fallbacks switch to another model when one fails. Logging helps debug prompts, and guardrails and key management features support security.

item.title: NVIDIA NIM
item.description:
NIM, short for NVIDIA Inference Microservices, packages a model so it is easy to deploy. Each microservice includes the model, optimized inference engines such as TensorRT-LLM, and standard APIs, delivered as a container. A team can run it on a cloud, a data center, or a workstation with NVIDIA GPUs and get tuned performance.

A catalog covers language models, vision, speech, and biology models from NVIDIA and partners, with APIs compatible with common formats such as OpenAI’s. Enterprises use NIM to keep models and data inside their environment while reaching production speed.

item.title: OpenVINO
item.description:
OpenVINO helps run models efficiently on Intel hardware. A developer takes a model from PyTorch, TensorFlow, or ONNX, converts it, and optimizes it with techniques like quantization, then runs it on CPUs, integrated and discrete GPUs, and neural processing units. This makes AI practical on laptops and edge devices without a high-end graphics card.

Newer parts target generative AI, including support for language models and image generation, with a GenAI library and integration with Hugging Face. Model servers and tools support deployment in applications.

item.title: Qualcomm AI Hub
item.description:
Qualcomm AI Hub targets on-device AI for phones, PCs, and other products built with Qualcomm chips. A developer uploads a model, and the service converts and optimizes it for the target hardware, then runs it on real devices in the cloud to measure speed and accuracy.

A library of ready-to-run models, such as vision, speech, and language models, saves time. Profiling shows where a model spends time and memory, guiding further tuning. The goal is to make it easy to run AI locally, with benefits for privacy, cost, and latency.

item.title: abab6.5
item.description: abab6.5 is a large language model from the Chinese company MiniMax, launched in April 2024 as the company’s flagship offering before it shifted toward open-weight releases with the M-series models. It runs on a mixture-of-experts architecture with a total parameter count in the trillions, though MiniMax has not disclosed exact figures, and it handles a 200,000-token context window. The lineup also included a companion model, abab6.5s, tuned for lower latency and cheaper inference at similar quality.

item.title: Act-One
item.description: Act-One is a feature inside Runway’s Gen-3 Alpha video model, released in October 2024, that turns an ordinary video of a person’s face into a driving signal for an AI-generated character. A creator films themselves on a phone or webcam, and Act-One maps their expressions, eye-lines, and timing onto a separate generated character without any motion-capture rig, facial markers, or manual keyframing. It supports multiple camera angles and can retarget a performance onto characters with different proportions from the original actor.

item.title: Amazon Nova Lite
item.description: Amazon Nova Lite is a multimodal model in Amazon’s Nova family, announced in December 2024 at AWS re:Invent and available through Amazon Bedrock. It accepts text, image, and video input and returns text output, with a 300,000-token context window, and is priced at $0.06 per million input tokens and $0.24 per million output tokens. Amazon built it as the mid-tier option between the text-only Nova Micro and the more capable Nova Pro, aimed at applications that need to handle images or video but still want fast response times and low cost.

item.title: Amazon Nova Micro
item.description: Amazon Nova Micro is the smallest and cheapest model in Amazon’s Nova lineup, announced in December 2024 alongside the rest of the family and available through Amazon Bedrock. It handles text only, in and out, with a 128,000-token context window, and is priced at $0.035 per million input tokens and $0.14 per million output tokens, making it Amazon’s answer to lightweight models like GPT-4o mini and Gemini Flash-Lite. Amazon built it for high-volume, latency-sensitive workloads such as text classification, simple extraction, and routing logic inside larger agent pipelines.

item.title: Amazon Nova Premier
item.description: Amazon Nova Premier is the most capable model in Amazon’s Nova family, sitting above Pro, Lite, and Micro, and it’s built for complex, multi-step reasoning and long-document agentic workflows on Amazon Bedrock. It takes text, image, and video input and offers a one-million-token context window, priced at $2.50 per million input tokens and $12.50 per million output tokens. Amazon designed it partly as a teacher model for Bedrock’s distillation pipeline, so customers can use Premier’s outputs to train cheaper Nova models for narrower production tasks.

item.title: Amazon Nova Pro
item.description: Amazon Nova Pro is the flagship general-purpose model in Amazon’s Nova family, announced in December 2024 and served through Amazon Bedrock. It takes text, image, and video input, returns text, and supports a 300,000-token context window, priced at $0.80 per million input tokens and $3.20 per million output tokens. Amazon positioned it as the model for complex tasks such as multi-step reasoning, document analysis, and agentic workflows where Nova Lite’s lighter capability isn’t enough.

item.title: Amazon Nova Sonic
item.description: Amazon Nova Sonic is a speech-to-speech model that Amazon announced in April 2025, unifying speech understanding and speech generation into a single model rather than chaining separate speech-to-text, language, and text-to-speech systems together. It’s accessed through a bidirectional streaming API on Amazon Bedrock, supports a 300,000-token context window, and is built for real-time voice agents that need to listen, reason, and respond with natural-sounding speech and low latency. It also supports tool use and knowledge grounding, so a voice agent built on Sonic can call external functions or retrieve information mid-conversation.

item.title: Baichuan 3
item.description: Baichuan 3 is a closed, API-only foundation model that Baichuan Intelligent Technology launched in January 2024, marking the point where the company stopped open-sourcing its flagship models and moved to a proprietary hosted service instead. Baichuan hasn’t disclosed the parameter count, though the company has said it improved on tasks like Chinese-language reasoning, code generation, and math over Baichuan 2, and claimed wins over GPT-4 on some Chinese benchmarks such as CMMLU and GAOKAO-style evaluations. It supports a 128K token context window and is accessed only through Baichuan’s API and chat product rather than downloadable weights. It sits between the open Baichuan 2 line and the more capable Baichuan 4 that followed later in 2024, and it was aimed mainly at enterprise customers inside China rather than at competing head-to-head with Western frontier models internationally.

item.title: Baichuan 4
item.description: Baichuan 4 is Baichuan Intelligent Technology’s flagship proprietary language model, with its API opened to developers in mid-2024. Like its predecessor Baichuan 3, the company hasn’t published a parameter count, but it has positioned the model around knowledge retrieval, long-context handling, and Chinese-language generation, and reported leading results on the domestic SuperCLUE benchmark. The family includes a Turbo variant tuned for enterprise deployment and an Air variant described as a mixture-of-experts model built for lower-cost inference, with Baichuan claiming the Turbo model priced at around 80% of GPT-4o’s API cost while offering comparable or better usability on Chinese tasks. It’s available only through Baichuan’s API and chat interface, with context windows reported up to 128K tokens in most deployments. Baichuan 4 competes mainly against other Chinese closed models like those from Alibaba’s Qwen team, Zhipu, and Moonshot rather than against Western frontier labs.

item.title: BGE-large-en
item.description: BGE-large-en-v1.5 is a text embedding model from BAAI, the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence, released in September 2023 as an update to the original BGE-large-en model from a few weeks earlier. It has 335 million parameters, produces 1024-dimension embeddings, and handles sequences up to 512 tokens, putting it in the same size class as other BERT-scale encoder models rather than the larger decoder-based embedding models that came later. The v1.5 update mainly fixed a similarity-score distribution issue in the original release and improved retrieval quality when used without a task-specific instruction prefix, which had been a rough edge in v1. BAAI released it under the MIT license, and it became one of the most widely used open embedding models for English retrieval and RAG pipelines, largely because it was free, fast to run, and scored well on the MTEB benchmark relative to its size. It’s since been joined by larger and more capable BAAI models like BGE-M3, but it remains a common default for lightweight self-hosted retrieval.

item.title: Claude 3 Opus
item.description: Claude 3 Opus was Anthropic’s flagship model when the Claude 3 family launched in March 2024, sitting above Sonnet and Haiku as the largest and most capable of the three. It handled complex analysis, long documents, and multi-step tasks better than any earlier Claude model, and at launch it beat GPT-4 on several public benchmarks, which helped establish Anthropic as a serious frontier lab rather than a distant second to OpenAI. It reads both text and images, supports a 200,000 token context window, and is priced at $15 per million input tokens and $75 per million output tokens, well above the Sonnet and Haiku tiers released alongside it. Anthropic has since shipped several generations of stronger, cheaper models, so Claude 3 Opus is now considered a legacy model rather than a current recommendation.

item.title: Claude 3 Sonnet
item.description: Claude 3 Sonnet is the middle tier of Anthropic’s original Claude 3 family, released in March 2024 alongside the smaller Haiku and the larger Opus. It was pitched as the balance point of the lineup: strong enough for most business tasks like summarization, coding help, and data analysis, but priced and sized to run more cheaply than Opus. At $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with a 200,000 token context window and support for image inputs, it became a common default for teams building on the Claude API in 2024. Anthropic replaced it a few months later with Claude 3.5 Sonnet, which outperformed it on most benchmarks at the same price, so Claude 3 Sonnet is now a legacy model.

item.title: Claude 3.5 Haiku
item.description: Claude 3.5 Haiku is Anthropic’s fast, low-cost model in the Claude 3.5 family, released in October 2024 alongside an upgraded Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Anthropic built it to replace Claude 3 Haiku as the cheapest, quickest option in the lineup while closing much of the capability gap with larger models: on coding evaluations such as SWE-bench Verified, Claude 3.5 Haiku scored competitively with the original Claude 3.5 Sonnet and outperformed several larger models available at launch, and Anthropic reported an 88.1% score on HumanEval for code generation.

item.title: Claude 3.5 Sonnet
item.description: Claude 3.5 Sonnet is a text-and-image language model from Anthropic, first released in June 2024 as a mid-tier upgrade to the Claude 3 lineup that matched or beat the larger Claude 3 Opus on most benchmarks while running faster and cheaper. Anthropic updated it again in October 2024 with a version that added computer use, a feature letting the model view a screenshot and control a mouse and keyboard to operate software the way a person would. That update made Claude 3.5 Sonnet one of the first widely available models built for agentic tasks like filling out web forms, navigating operating systems, and running multi-step workflows without a human clicking each button. It kept the 200,000 token context window of its predecessors and priced at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, positioning it as Anthropic’s workhorse model through much of 2024 and early 2025 before the Claude 3.7 and Claude 4 lines replaced it.

item.title: Claude 3.7 Sonnet
item.description: Claude 3.7 Sonnet, released by Anthropic in February 2025, is the company’s first hybrid reasoning model. A single model can answer normally like a standard chat model or switch into an extended thinking mode where it works through a problem step by step before responding, and developers can control how much thinking budget the model uses through the API. This design let Anthropic ship one model that covers both quick everyday questions and harder math, coding, and logic problems, instead of maintaining separate fast and reasoning-focused models. It kept the same 200,000 token context window and $3/$15 per million token pricing as Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and it launched alongside Claude Code, Anthropic’s command-line coding agent, which used 3.7 Sonnet as its default model.

item.title: Claude Fable 5
item.description: Claude Fable 5 is a public, safety-restricted release of Mythos, an internal Anthropic model class that the company unveiled in April 2026 and initially withheld from general availability because of its advanced cybersecurity capabilities. Anthropic made Fable 5 available to enterprise customers and paid subscribers on June 9, 2026, after adding safeguards that redirect queries in high-risk areas like cybersecurity and biology to Claude Opus 4.8 instead, a mechanism the company says triggers in under 5 percent of sessions. On paper it is the strongest model Anthropic has shipped publicly: 95.0 percent on SWE-bench Verified, 80.3 percent on the harder SWE-bench Pro, and 92.6 percent on GPQA Diamond, with strong results in vision and scientific research tasks as well. It carries a 1 million token context window and is priced at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens, double what Anthropic charges for Opus 4.8, reflecting its positioning as a specialty top-tier option rather than a general daily driver.

item.title: Claude Haiku 4.5
item.description: Claude Haiku 4.5 is Anthropic’s fastest and cheapest current-generation model, released on October 15, 2025. It is the first Haiku model to include extended thinking, computer use, and context awareness, features that had previously only shipped in Anthropic’s larger Sonnet and Opus models. On SWE-bench Verified it scores about 73.3 percent, which puts it within a few points of Claude Sonnet 4.5’s 77.2 percent despite costing a third as much: $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens versus Sonnet’s $3/$15. That makes it a practical choice for running many agents in parallel or handling high-volume tasks where Sonnet or Opus would be needlessly expensive. It reads both text and images and shares the 200,000 token context window used across the rest of the current Claude lineup.

item.title: Claude Opus 4
item.description: Claude Opus 4 launched on May 22, 2025 as Anthropic’s flagship model, released alongside the smaller Claude Sonnet 4. It was built for sustained, long-horizon agentic work such as multi-hour coding sessions and research tasks that involve using tools repeatedly across a long thread, rather than answering a single prompt. Anthropic reported it leading on SWE-bench Verified at launch, at roughly 72.5 percent, and it can use tools, including web search, during extended thinking and run several tools in parallel. It runs on a 200,000 token context window, reads images as well as text, and is priced at $15 per million input tokens and $75 per million output tokens, the same rate Anthropic had charged for Claude 3 Opus a year earlier.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.1
item.description: Claude Opus 4.1, released in August 2025, is a targeted update to Claude Opus 4 rather than a new generation. Anthropic focused the update on coding and agentic accuracy, and it pushed the SWE-bench Verified score up to roughly 74.5 percent, a meaningful jump on the real-world GitHub issue benchmark that Anthropic uses to track coding ability. It kept the same 200,000 token context window, image input support, and $15/$75 per million token pricing as Opus 4, and it gained the ability to use up to 64,000 tokens of extended thinking for harder problems. Anthropic described it as a drop-in replacement for Opus 4, meant to hold the top of the Opus line until the next full model generation shipped.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.8
item.description: Claude Opus 4.8 is Anthropic’s most capable Opus-tier model, released on May 28, 2026 as an update to Opus 4.7 that fixed some of that model’s comment-verbosity and tool-calling quirks. It scores about 88.6 percent on SWE-bench Verified and 69.2 percent on the harder SWE-bench Pro, ahead of GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro on the same test at the time of release, and Anthropic reports it is more likely to flag its own uncertainty rather than state unsupported claims with confidence. It supports a 1 million token input context window with up to 128,000 tokens of output, and it introduced Dynamic Workflows, a research-preview feature in Claude Code that lets the model plan a large task and then run hundreds of parallel subagents in a single session. Pricing held steady from the previous version at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, with a faster “fast mode” available at $10/$50.

item.title: Claude Sonnet 4
item.description: Claude Sonnet 4 launched on May 22, 2025 alongside the larger Claude Opus 4, taking the mid-tier spot in Anthropic’s Claude 4 generation. It is a hybrid reasoning model, meaning it can answer directly or work through a problem step by step in an extended thinking mode depending on the task, and Anthropic reported it hitting roughly 72.7 percent on SWE-bench Verified at launch, edging out even Opus 4 on that particular benchmark while costing a fraction of the price. It ships with a 200,000 token context window as standard, with a 1 million token context window available in beta on the API and Amazon Bedrock, and it reads images alongside text. At $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, it became Anthropic’s default recommendation for coding and everyday agentic work where Opus-level cost isn’t justified.

item.title: Claude Sonnet 4.5
item.description: Claude Sonnet 4.5, released on September 29, 2025, was Anthropic’s highest-scoring Sonnet-tier model on SWE-bench Verified at launch, reaching about 77.2 percent on the full 500-problem set with extended thinking enabled. Anthropic built it heavily around coding and computer use, and testers reported it staying focused on a single complex task for more than 30 hours without losing track of what it was doing. It added context awareness, meaning the model tracks how much of its context window remains during a long conversation and adjusts its behavior as it fills up, which matters for agents running long unattended sessions. It kept Sonnet’s $3/$15 per million token pricing and 200,000 token standard context window, with a 1 million token context window available in beta, making it Anthropic’s primary recommendation for coding agents and long-running automation through the rest of 2025.

item.title: Claude Sonnet 5
item.description: Claude Sonnet 5 launched on June 30, 2026 as Anthropic’s most agentic Sonnet model yet, built to plan multi-step tasks and use tools like browsers and terminals with less hand-holding than earlier Sonnet versions. It performs close to Claude Opus 4.8 on most benchmarks, including roughly 85.2 percent on SWE-bench Verified and 63.2 percent on SWE-bench Pro, while costing noticeably less, which is why Anthropic and reviewers have framed it as a cheaper way to run coding agents at scale. It carries a 1 million token context window with context compaction to manage long agent sessions, and reads both text and images. Anthropic priced it at an introductory $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through August 31, 2026, after which it moves to standard pricing of $3/$15, and it is now the default model for free and Pro Claude.ai plans.

item.title: Codestral
item.description: Codestral is Mistral AI’s dedicated code generation model, first released in May 2024 with 22 billion parameters. It’s built for fill-in-the-middle completion and multi-language code generation, and it launched with an 81.1 percent pass@1 score on HumanEval, ahead of larger code models like Code Llama 70B and DeepSeek Coder 33B at the time. The original release used a 32,000-token context window and shipped under the Mistral AI Non-Production License, which limited free use to research and testing and required a separate commercial license for production deployment.

item.title: Codestral Mamba
item.description: Codestral Mamba is a code generation model Mistral AI released in July 2024, notable mainly for its architecture: instead of the transformer design used by nearly every other code model, it’s built on Mamba, a state-space model architecture. State-space models process sequences with linear rather than quadratic scaling in sequence length, which means inference speed does not degrade as sharply as context grows. Mistral sized it at roughly 7 billion parameters and gave it a 256,000-token context window, with the company reporting reliable in-context retrieval performance even at that length.

item.title: CogVideoX
item.description: CogVideoX is Zhipu AI’s open-weight text-to-video model, built with Tsinghua University’s KEG lab and released in August 2024 as a successor to the original CogVideo project. It ships in 2B and 5B parameter variants using a 3D causal VAE for spatial and temporal compression alongside an expert adaptive LayerNorm transformer, and it supports text-to-video, image-to-video, and video continuation from a single frame or prompt. The 5B model generates clips up to 10 seconds long at up to 768p resolution and 16 frames per second, and Zhipu later shipped a CogVideoX-1.5 update in November 2024 with longer, higher-resolution output. Weights are released under Apache 2.0 and hosted on Hugging Face, and Zhipu also serves the models through its own API, so CogVideoX works both as a self-hosted open model and as a hosted service, similar to how Stability AI and Runway position their video generators.

item.title: CogView3
item.description: CogView3 is a text-to-image model from Zhipu AI and Tsinghua University, described in a March 2024 research paper and open-sourced on Hugging Face in September 2024. It is built around relay diffusion, a cascaded approach where a 3-billion-parameter base stage generates a low-resolution 512x512 image and a second stage adds noise back into that image before running a shorter super-resolution diffusion pass on top of it, rather than conditioning the second stage directly on the low-res output like older cascaded models did. Zhipu reports that CogView3 beats Stable Diffusion XL in human evaluations by a wide margin while needing only about half the inference time, and a distilled version matches that quality using roughly a tenth of SDXL’s inference steps. The model and code are released under Apache 2.0, and Zhipu followed it with CogView-3Plus, a larger diffusion transformer variant in the same family, plus a hosted version through the Zhipu API for developers who don’t want to run it themselves.

item.title: Cohere Embed Multilingual v3
item.description: Cohere Embed Multilingual v3 is a text embedding model Cohere released in November 2023 for search, retrieval-augmented generation, and semantic similarity tasks across more than 100 languages. It takes input text up to 512 tokens and outputs a 1024-dimension vector by default, with support for shorter 384 or 768 dimension embeddings when a team wants faster search or lower storage cost. Cohere trained it alongside an English-only sibling, Embed English v3, and pitched both as an upgrade over v2 because they weight passages by how relevant they are likely to be, not just how similar they are, which cuts down on noisy retrieval results in RAG pipelines. It’s priced at $0.10 per million tokens through the Cohere API and is also distributed through AWS, Azure, and Oracle Cloud marketplaces. Cohere has since released newer Embed v4 models, and some cloud providers such as Oracle now list v3 as a legacy or deprecated option, though it remains available through Cohere’s own API and Hugging Face.

item.title: Cohere Embed v3
item.description: Cohere Embed v3 is a text embedding model that Cohere released in November 2023 for search, retrieval-augmented generation, and semantic search applications. It comes in English and multilingual variants, and the multilingual version was trained on over 100 languages and improved retrieval accuracy on the MIRACL benchmark by roughly 35% over the previous generation. The model lets a caller specify whether a text is a search query or a document, which adjusts the embedding space to improve retrieval accuracy.
