It’s available only through Cohere’s API, priced at $0.10 per million input tokens, and accepts inputs up to 512 tokens. Embed v3 became a standard choice for RAG pipelines alongside OpenAI’s text-embedding-3 and Voyage AI’s embedding models, before Cohere introduced the multimodal Embed v4 in 2025.

item.title: Cohere Embed v4
item.description: Cohere Embed v4 is Cohere’s multimodal embedding model, released in April 2025 as the successor to Embed v3. Unlike its predecessor, it accepts text, images, and mixed documents in a single call and produces a unified vector representation, so a screenshot of a PDF page, a slide, or a table can be indexed directly alongside plain text without first converting it to text. It supports a 128,000 token context window, well beyond OpenAI’s and Voyage’s embedding models, and offers Matryoshka embeddings at 256, 512, 1024, or 1536 dimensions so users can trade storage against accuracy. Pricing is $0.12 per million text tokens and $0.47 per million image tokens through the Cohere API, and the model is also available on Amazon Bedrock and Azure AI. Cohere positions it for enterprise document search and RAG systems that need to handle scanned or visually formatted content, not just plain text.

item.title: Command A
item.description: Command A is Cohere’s flagship large language model, released in March 2025 at the top of its Command lineup. It has 111 billion parameters and a 256,000 token context window, and Cohere built it to run on as few as two GPUs while matching or beating larger competing models on agentic, multilingual, and coding tasks. It scores 85.5 on MMLU, putting it in the same range as GPT-4o and Llama 3.3 70B. Command A is tuned for retrieval-augmented generation and tool use, and it’s available through the Cohere platform and Azure AI at $2.50 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, or as a self-hosted deployment for enterprises that need to keep data on their own infrastructure. Cohere later added Command A+, a larger 218 billion parameter model, to the same family.

item.title: Command R Plus
item.description: Command R Plus is Cohere’s flagship model from the Command R generation, released in April 2024 with a 128,000 token context window and 104 billion parameters. Cohere built it for retrieval-augmented generation, multi-step tool use, and multilingual tasks, and launched it in partnership with Microsoft Azure as one of the first models in that generation to pair strong RAG performance with agentic tool calling. The model scores 75.7 on MMLU. Cohere published the weights on Hugging Face under a CC-BY-NC 4.0 license with an acceptable use addendum, so researchers can download and run it for non-commercial purposes for free, while commercial use requires a separate license or access through Cohere’s hosted API at $2.50 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. It sits above the smaller Command R model in Cohere’s lineup and was superseded by Command A in 2025.

item.title: CosyVoice
item.description: CosyVoice is a text-to-speech and voice-cloning model from Alibaba’s FunAudioLLM team, released as open weights in July 2024. It generates speech from short reference audio clips, so it can clone a voice from just a few seconds of sample and then speak arbitrary text in that voice across multiple languages, including Chinese, English, Japanese, and Korean. The model builds on supervised semantic speech tokens paired with a language-model-style generation approach, which lets it handle cross-lingual and zero-shot voice cloning without speaker-specific fine-tuning. Alibaba has continued to update the line, later releasing CosyVoice 2 and CosyVoice 3 with larger underlying models and lower latency, and the original release remains available on Hugging Face and through Alibaba Cloud’s Model Studio API under an Apache 2.0 license.

item.title: DALL-E 2
item.description: DALL-E 2 is OpenAI’s second text-to-image model, announced in April 2022. Unlike the original DALL-E, it switched from an autoregressive transformer to a diffusion-based architecture, using roughly 3.5 billion parameters for the core model plus another 1.5 billion for the upsamplers that sharpen output resolution. It generated images at four times the resolution of its predecessor and introduced inpainting and outpainting, letting users edit parts of an existing image or extend it beyond its original borders. DALL-E 2’s viral demos of photorealistic and stylized images helped push text-to-image generation into mainstream awareness well before ChatGPT existed, and it opened to the public in 2022 after an initial waitlist period. OpenAI has since folded image generation into DALL-E 3 and its GPT-image models, and DALL-E 2 remains available mainly for legacy API access.

item.title: DALL-E 3
item.description: DALL-E 3 is OpenAI’s third-generation image model, released in October 2023 with tight integration into ChatGPT. Instead of requiring users to hand-craft detailed prompts, it uses ChatGPT to expand short requests into fuller descriptions before generating the image, which noticeably improved prompt adherence and text rendering compared to DALL-E 2. OpenAI has not disclosed the model’s parameter count or training details, publishing only a technical report focused on how it was trained to follow instructions more closely, including techniques to reduce the model’s tendency to ignore parts of a prompt. It is accessible through ChatGPT Plus and Enterprise plans as well as the OpenAI API, and it competes with models like Midjourney and Google’s Imagen line on prompt fidelity and image quality. OpenAI has since moved its focus to newer image models, so DALL-E 3 is now considered a legacy offering still in production use.

item.title: DeepSeek-Coder-33B
item.description: DeepSeek-Coder-33B is a code-focused language model that DeepSeek released in November 2023, before the company became widely known for its later reasoning models. It was trained from scratch on 2 trillion tokens split mostly between code and natural language, with a 16,000-token context window and project-level training that lets it reason across multiple files rather than isolated snippets. The instruction-tuned version scored 79.3% pass@1 on HumanEval at release, putting it ahead of most open code models of the time and within striking distance of GPT-3.5 on coding benchmarks. It supports fill-in-the-middle completion for use in code editors and covers a wide range of programming languages. DeepSeek has since superseded it with DeepSeek-Coder-V2, a larger mixture-of-experts model with a longer context window, but the 33B model is still available on Hugging Face for self-hosting.

item.title: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B
item.description: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B is a distilled reasoning model DeepSeek released alongside DeepSeek-R1 in January 2025. Rather than training a reasoning model from scratch, DeepSeek fine-tuned Meta’s Llama 3.3 70B Instruct on reasoning traces generated by the full R1 model, transferring much of R1’s chain-of-thought problem-solving ability into a smaller, cheaper-to-run architecture. It is the largest of six distilled R1 variants DeepSeek published, spanning Qwen and Llama base models from 1.5B up to 70B parameters, and on release it scored 70.0% pass@1 on AIME 2024 and 94.5% on MATH-500, far ahead of general-purpose models like GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet on the same math benchmarks. It carries a 128,000-token context window, inherited from its Llama 3.3 base, and is distributed under the Llama 3.3 Community License, with weights on Hugging Face and hosted API access through providers including Together AI.

item.title: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B
item.description: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B is a dense 32-billion-parameter model that DeepSeek built by fine-tuning Qwen2.5-32B on reasoning traces generated by the full DeepSeek-R1 model. Rather than training a smaller model from scratch, DeepSeek distilled R1’s chain-of-thought outputs into several base models, and the 32B Qwen version turned out to be the strongest of the group. It beat OpenAI’s o1-mini on math, coding, and science benchmarks despite its comparatively modest size, which made it one of the first open models small enough to run on a single high-end GPU while still showing real reasoning ability. The weights are released under the MIT license alongside the rest of the R1 family, and the model is widely mirrored on Hugging Face and served by inference providers such as Together AI and Groq.

item.title: Devstral
item.description: Devstral is a 24-billion-parameter code model that Mistral AI released on May 21, 2025, built in collaboration with All Hands AI, the team behind the OpenHands agent framework. Unlike most code models, which are tuned mainly for autocomplete or single-turn code generation, Devstral is trained specifically for agentic coding: exploring a codebase across multiple files, using tools, and completing multi-step software engineering tasks. On SWE-bench Verified it scored 46.8%, ahead of every open model available at release and even some larger proprietary ones.

item.title: Doubao 1.5 Pro
item.description: Doubao 1.5 Pro is ByteDance’s flagship foundation model, launched on January 22, 2025 through its Volcano Engine cloud platform and the Doubao consumer assistant app. It uses a sparse mixture-of-experts architecture that ByteDance says delivers performance comparable to a dense model roughly seven times its active parameter count, and it ships in both a 32K and a 256K context-window variant. ByteDance reported that it matched or beat GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet on a range of benchmarks, including math and reasoning tests, while pricing its API at a fraction of what those competitors charged.

item.title: Doubao Vision
item.description: Doubao Vision is ByteDance’s multimodal tier for image and document understanding, launched on December 18, 2024 at Volcano Engine’s Force conference. It reads and reasons over visual content: identifying objects, analyzing charts, working through logic problems posed as images, reading code from screenshots, and answering questions tied to a picture rather than only describing it. ByteDance built it as part of the broader Doubao model family that powers its consumer assistant app and its Volcano Engine cloud API.

item.title: Doubao-Seed 1.6
item.description: Doubao-Seed 1.6 is ByteDance’s reasoning-tuned model tier, announced on June 11, 2025 at Volcano Engine’s “Force” conference alongside two variants, Doubao-Seed-1.6-thinking and the lighter Doubao-Seed-1.6-flash. It supports a 256K context window and native multimodal understanding of text, images, and video within a single model, along with a configurable thinking mode that lets developers trade off latency against reasoning depth. ByteDance reported strong results on complex reasoning and competition-level math benchmarks compared to the earlier Doubao 1.5 generation.

item.title: Eleven Flash v2.5
item.description: Eleven Flash v2.5 is ElevenLabs’ fastest text-to-speech model, built for voice agents and other applications where response time matters more than raw audio polish. It generates speech in about 75 milliseconds, not counting network and application overhead, and covers 32 languages including additions like Hungarian, Norwegian, and Vietnamese that weren’t in the earlier Flash v2. ElevenLabs prices it at roughly half the cost per character of its flagship Multilingual v2 model, which makes it the default choice for conversational AI products, live customer support bots, and other real-time voice interfaces where a 300-millisecond model would feel sluggish. The tradeoff is expressiveness: Flash v2.5 sounds clean and fast but doesn’t carry the emotional range ElevenLabs built into Eleven v3.

item.title: Eleven Multilingual v2
item.description: Eleven Multilingual v2 is the speech synthesis model ElevenLabs shipped when it moved its text-to-speech product out of beta, in August 2023. It generates natural-sounding speech across 29 languages, including Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, Hindi, and most major European languages, while preserving a cloned voice’s character between languages. Compared to ElevenLabs’ faster Flash and Turbo models, Multilingual v2 trades speed for quality: it’s meant for narration, dubbing, audiobooks, and other content where the audio gets published rather than streamed live in a conversation. It remains one of ElevenLabs’ most widely used models for voice cloning and dubbing workflows even after the company released Eleven v3.

item.title: Eleven Turbo v2.5
item.description: Eleven Turbo v2.5 sits between ElevenLabs’ Flash and Multilingual models, aiming for a middle ground of roughly 250 to 300 millisecond latency with better audio quality than Flash. It supports 32 languages, including Vietnamese, Hungarian, and Norwegian, which were new additions over the original Turbo v2, and generates speech about three times faster than Multilingual v2 for non-English text. ElevenLabs recommends it for applications that need decent responsiveness but can tolerate a bit more delay than a live phone call, such as chat-based assistants or interactive tools where the reply doesn’t have to feel instantaneous. It’s functionally similar to Flash v2.5 in capability but consistently runs a bit slower in practice.

item.title: Eleven v3
item.description: Eleven v3 is ElevenLabs’ most expressive text-to-speech model, launched in public alpha on June 5, 2025 and moved to general availability in March 2026. It supports over 70 languages and introduces inline audio tags such as [excited], [whispers], [sighs], and [laughing], which let a user script a voice performance rather than just its words, plus multi-speaker dialogue generation for conversations between different voices. The model is built for content where emotional delivery matters, like audiobooks, game characters, and narrative ads, rather than for the low-latency conversational use cases that Flash and Turbo cover. Because it prioritizes expressiveness over speed, ElevenLabs positions it as a separate track from its real-time voice agent models rather than a straight replacement for them.

item.title: ERNIE 4.0
item.description: ERNIE 4.0 is the large language model Baidu introduced in October 2023 as the engine behind its Ernie Bot chatbot, positioned at the time as Baidu’s answer to GPT-4. Baidu never disclosed its parameter count or training details, keeping it a closed, proprietary model accessible only through Baidu Cloud’s API and the Ernie Bot app rather than as downloadable weights. It handles Chinese and English text generation, reasoning, and multi-turn conversation, and Baidu later added a “Turbo” variant that improved speed and cost. ERNIE 4.0 has since been superseded by ERNIE 4.5, which Baidu released as an open-weight model family in 2025, and by ERNIE 5.0.

item.title: Firefly Image 3
item.description: Firefly Image 3 is Adobe’s image generation model, introduced in April 2024 as an upgrade over the original Firefly model that launched in 2023. Adobe trained it to be commercially safe, meaning it draws only on licensed Adobe Stock content, public domain material, and other content Adobe has rights to use, which lets business customers generate images without the copyright uncertainty tied to models trained on scraped web data. It improved on its predecessor with better prompt understanding, sharper detail, and Structure Reference and Style Reference tools that let users guide output using an existing image’s composition or visual style. Adobe built it into Photoshop, Illustrator, Adobe Express, and the standalone Firefly web app, with API access for enterprise integrations. Adobe has continued to ship newer Firefly image models since, and it retired Image 3 from its model picker in 2026 in favor of those successors.

item.title: Firefly Vector
item.description: Firefly Vector is Adobe’s generative model for producing editable vector graphics from text prompts, first shown at Adobe MAX in October 2023 as a beta feature inside Illustrator. Adobe describes it as the first generative AI model built specifically for vector output rather than raster images, which matters because vector graphics need to stay editable as paths and shapes rather than fixed pixels. It powers Illustrator features like Text to Vector Graphic, Generative Shape Fill, Generative Recolor, and Text to Pattern, letting designers generate logos, icons, and patterns they can still resize and edit like any other vector artwork. Like the rest of the Firefly line, it trains only on licensed and public domain content so outputs are safe for commercial use. Adobe has kept expanding the model’s capabilities through Illustrator’s regular feature updates rather than treating it as a single fixed release.

item.title: Firefly Video
item.description: Firefly Video is Adobe’s text-to-video and image-to-video model, announced at Adobe MAX in October 2024 and opened to public beta through the standalone Firefly web app in February 2025. Adobe positions it as the first widely available video model built to be commercially safe, trained on licensed and public domain sources so businesses can use its output without copyright exposure. Inside Premiere Pro, it powers Generative Extend, a feature editors use to stretch a clip to cover a gap in footage, smooth a jump cut, or hold a shot longer without reshooting. Through 2025, Adobe added camera motion controls, start-frame image uploads, and prompt-based editing of existing footage, moving the tool from pure generation toward directed video editing. It remains in beta as of mid-2026, with Adobe rolling out updates alongside its other Firefly models rather than shipping a single finished version.

item.title: FLUX.1 Kontext
item.description: FLUX.1 Kontext is Black Forest Labs’ image editing model, announced on May 29, 2025 as an extension of the base FLUX line into instruction-based editing. Instead of only generating images from text, Kontext takes both a text instruction and a reference image, then applies targeted edits, such as changing an object, adjusting lighting, or transforming part of a scene, while keeping the rest of the image and the subject’s identity consistent. Black Forest Labs released it in multiple tiers: a closed Pro version and a faster Max version accessible through its API and partners like fal.ai, plus an open-weight Kontext dev model with 12 billion parameters that Hugging Face users can run themselves under a non-commercial license. The company markets its inference speed as up to eight times faster than comparable editing models at the time of release. Kontext competes directly with instruction-based editing features in Google’s Gemini image models and OpenAI’s image tools, an area that saw heavy competition through 2025.

item.title: FLUX.1 Krea
item.description: FLUX.1 Krea is a text-to-image model Black Forest Labs built together with Krea, an AI creative tools startup, and released as open weights on July 31, 2025. The two companies designed it specifically to avoid the oversaturated, overly smooth look common to many diffusion models, aiming instead for more photorealistic, less obviously AI-generated output. It’s a 12 billion parameter rectified-flow model distilled from Krea’s own Krea 1 model, and it’s built to be compatible with the existing FLUX.1 dev ecosystem, so tools, LoRAs, and workflows built around FLUX.1 dev work with it directly. Black Forest Labs released the dev version on Hugging Face under its non-commercial license, with commercial use requiring a separate license through BFL’s portal. The collaboration reflects a broader pattern in image generation during 2025, where model labs partnered with product-focused startups to fix a specific complaint from users: that AI images all started to look the same.

item.title: FLUX.1 Pro
item.description: FLUX.1 Pro is the flagship, closed-weight model in Black Forest Labs’ FLUX family, released in August 2024 alongside the open FLUX.1 dev and schnell tiers. It’s a 12 billion parameter rectified flow transformer, the largest and highest-quality version in the lineup, available only through Black Forest Labs’ own API and hosting partners such as Replicate and fal.ai rather than as downloadable weights. Black Forest Labs was founded in 2024 by researchers who previously built Stable Diffusion at Stability AI, and FLUX quickly became one of the strongest text-to-image models for prompt adherence, typography, and image composition, competing with Midjourney and OpenAI’s image models. Pricing is usage-based per generated image rather than a flat subscription, aimed at developers building image generation into products rather than casual end users. Since the initial release, Black Forest Labs has layered additional Pro-tier capabilities on top, including the Kontext editing models, while keeping FLUX.1 Pro as the general-purpose flagship for straight text-to-image generation.

item.title: Gemini 1.5 Flash
item.description: Gemini 1.5 Flash is Google’s fast, low-cost tier of the Gemini 1.5 generation, released in May 2024 as a distilled version of Gemini 1.5 Pro. Google built it by teaching a smaller model to imitate Pro’s outputs, which kept much of Pro’s reasoning ability while cutting latency and cost sharply. It carries the same million-token context window as Pro and handles text, images, audio, and video, making it a practical choice for high-volume tasks like summarizing long documents or captioning video where Pro’s price would add up quickly.

item.title: Gemini 1.5 Pro
item.description: Gemini 1.5 Pro is the model that introduced million-token context windows to a mainstream API, released by Google in February 2024 and moved to general availability that May. It reads text, images, audio, and video in a single prompt, and Google demonstrated it holding an entire hour of video or hundreds of pages of documents in context at once, well beyond what GPT-4 or Claude offered at the time. It uses a mixture-of-experts architecture, which Google said let it match or beat the larger Gemini 1.0 Ultra on most benchmarks while running cheaper.

item.title: Gemini 2.0 Flash
item.description: Gemini 2.0 Flash is Google’s low-latency multimodal model from the 2.0 generation, first previewed in December 2024 and moved to general availability on February 5, 2025. It takes text, images, audio, and video as input and can produce text, image, and audio output, with a million-token context window and native support for tool use like search and code execution. Google built it as the workhorse tier of the 2.0 family, positioned to outperform the older 1.5 Pro on many benchmarks while running faster and cheaper.

item.title: Gemini 2.5 Flash
item.description: Gemini 2.5 Flash is Google’s cost-efficient tier of the 2.5 generation, released as a preview in April 2025 and moved to general availability the following month. It’s the first Flash model built with visible thinking built in from the start: it can reason step by step through a problem before answering, and developers can set a “thinking budget” to trade off answer quality against latency and cost. It takes text, image, and audio input and handles the same million-token context window as its Pro sibling.

item.title: Gemini 2.5 Pro
item.description: Gemini 2.5 Pro is Google’s reasoning-focused flagship from the 2.5 generation, released as a preview on March 25, 2025 and reaching general availability that June. It’s a “thinking” model by default, meaning it works through problems step by step internally before producing a final answer, and it handles text, image, audio, and video across a million-token context window. At launch, Google positioned it as its strongest model yet for math, science, and coding tasks, and it topped several public leaderboards including LMArena.

item.title: Gemini 3 Pro
item.description: Gemini 3 Pro is Google’s flagship model, announced November 18, 2025 as the successor to Gemini 2.5 Pro. It reads and generates across text, image, audio, and video, with a 1 million token input context window and up to 64,000 tokens of output, and it launched with strong claims on math, science, and agentic benchmarks. On release it broke 1500 Elo on the LMArena leaderboard, reaching 1501 and taking the top public ranking, and Google reported it scoring well ahead of rival models on multimodal understanding tests like MMMU-Pro.

item.title: Gemini 3.5 Pro
item.description: Gemini 3.5 Pro is the high-end model in Google’s next Gemini generation, following Gemini 3 Pro and its 3.1 Pro update. Google announced it at I/O in May 2026 alongside Gemini 3.5 Flash, which reached general availability first. As of mid-July 2026, Gemini 3.5 Pro itself is still not broadly available: Google has confirmed the model is real and in internal use, with a small number of enterprise testers given early access through a developer platform, but the company has not published a model card, final pricing, or a firm release date.

item.title: Gemini Embedding
item.description: Gemini Embedding is Google’s text embedding model, built from the Gemini family and made generally available through the Gemini API starting in March 2025. It converts text into a single vector representation that developers use for search, clustering, classification, and retrieval-augmented generation, replacing Google’s earlier separate embedding models with one unified model trained across over 100 languages plus code. It supports Matryoshka Representation Learning, so a developer can truncate the default embedding down to smaller sizes like 768 or 256 dimensions to save storage without retraining anything.

item.title: GLM-4-Plus
item.description:
GLM-4-Plus is Zhipu AI’s proprietary flagship model, announced at the KDD 2024 conference and made available at the end of August 2024. It sits alongside the open-weight GLM-4 release as the closed, higher-capability tier, aimed at complex reasoning, long-text handling, and instruction following in both Chinese and English. It supports a 128,000-token context window and is accessed only through Zhipu’s own API platform, with no downloadable weights.

At launch, Zhipu positioned it as comparable to GPT-4 on a range of Chinese and English benchmarks, and it was among the first models from the company to add consumer-facing video call features. Because parameter counts for the model were never disclosed, it’s best understood as Zhipu’s answer to OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s paid flagship tiers rather than as a research artifact, sold on capability and price rather than openness.

item.title: GPT-3.5 Turbo
item.description: GPT-3.5 Turbo is the model OpenAI put behind ChatGPT when it launched to the public in November 2022, and it became a standalone API product on March 1, 2023. It’s a cheaper, faster variant of the GPT-3 line, tuned with instruction following and reinforcement learning from human feedback rather than raw few-shot completion. The original API version had a 4,096-token context window; a 16,000-token variant followed for customers who needed longer conversations or documents.

item.title: GPT-4
item.description: GPT-4 is OpenAI’s large language model launched on March 14, 2023, roughly four months after ChatGPT put the company on the map. It was the first GPT model to accept image input alongside text, and it passed a simulated bar exam near the 90th percentile, a result OpenAI used to argue the model had moved past the pattern-matching feel of GPT-3.5. The initial release shipped with an 8K token context window, with a 32K version available to select API customers. GPT-4 held OpenAI’s flagship spot for over a year, until GPT-4o replaced it in May 2024 with faster, cheaper, natively multimodal generation. It is still available through the API and ChatGPT today, mostly for backward compatibility, though OpenAI has pointed developers toward GPT-4.1 and later models for new projects.

item.title: GPT-4 Turbo
item.description: GPT-4 Turbo is OpenAI’s November 2023 update to GPT-4, announced at the company’s first developer conference. It kept GPT-4’s underlying capability level but expanded the context window to 128,000 tokens, added a knowledge cutoff of April 2023, and cut pricing to $10 per million input tokens and $30 per million output tokens, well below original GPT-4 rates. It scores 86.5% on MMLU and 87.1% on HumanEval, and it added vision input, letting developers send images alongside text in the same request.

item.title: GPT-4.1
item.description:
GPT-4.1 is OpenAI’s April 2025 model, released as an API-only update aimed squarely at developers rather than ChatGPT users. Its headline feature is a 1-million-token context window across all three variants, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 Mini, and GPT-4.1 Nano, an eightfold jump over GPT-4o’s 128,000 tokens. It scores 80.1% on MMLU and 54.6% on SWE-bench Verified, a 21-point improvement over GPT-4o on real-world software engineering tasks pulled from GitHub issues.

OpenAI priced the flagship variant at $2 per million input tokens and $8 per million output tokens, about 26% cheaper than GPT-4o, while GPT-4.1 Mini undercuts GPT-4o by roughly 83% on many benchmarks. The combination of long context and coding performance made it popular quickly for tools that need to process large codebases or long documents in a single pass, and it effectively replaced GPT-4.5 as OpenAI’s recommended model for API use later in 2025.

item.title: GPT-4.5
item.description: GPT-4.5 is OpenAI’s largest model released before GPT-5, launched on February 27, 2025 for ChatGPT Plus and Pro subscribers and, briefly, through the API. OpenAI described it as trained with a focus on natural conversation and broad world knowledge rather than step-by-step reasoning, and it outperformed GPT-4o on multilingual MMLU testing across the fifteen languages OpenAI checked. Its parameter count was never disclosed, and its context window stayed at 128,000 tokens, unchanged from GPT-4-class models before it.

item.title: GPT-4o
item.description: GPT-4o (“omni”) is the model OpenAI unveiled on May 13, 2024, as the successor to GPT-4 and the first in the line built from the ground up to handle text, images, and audio in a single network rather than bolting separate models together. It became the default model behind ChatGPT and cut API pricing roughly in half compared to GPT-4 Turbo, at $2.50 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, while also doubling generation speed. On launch benchmarks it scored 88.7 on MMLU and 90.2 on HumanEval, putting it ahead of GPT-4 on most reasoning and coding tests, and its live demo of real-time voice conversation and vision (reading facial expressions, solving handwritten math problems on camera) was the centerpiece of OpenAI’s spring 2024 announcement. GPT-4o remained OpenAI’s flagship for over a year before GPT-5 took over the position in August 2025, and it is still offered through the API and Azure OpenAI for existing integrations.

item.title: GPT-4o mini
item.description: GPT-4o mini is OpenAI’s small multimodal model, released July 18, 2024, as a cheaper replacement for GPT-3.5 Turbo in the API and free tier of ChatGPT. It takes text and image input, holds a 128K token context window, and costs 15 cents per million input tokens and 60 cents per million output tokens, a fraction of what the full GPT-4o charges. Despite the small footprint, it scored 82.0 on MMLU and 87.2 on HumanEval at launch, beating comparable small models from Google and Anthropic on most published benchmarks at the time. OpenAI positioned it for high-volume tasks like customer support, content moderation, and simple coding assistance where GPT-4o-level reasoning is not worth the extra cost. It has since been layered under successive OpenAI releases, but its price point kept it in wide use among developers building cost-sensitive applications.

item.title: GPT-4o Realtime
item.description: GPT-4o Realtime is a speech-to-speech variant of GPT-4o that OpenAI introduced through its Realtime API on October 1, 2024. Instead of the usual pipeline of transcribing audio to text, running it through a language model, and synthesizing speech back out, it processes audio natively end to end over a WebSocket or WebRTC connection, which cuts the lag that made earlier voice bots feel stilted. It powers ChatGPT’s Advanced Voice Mode and lets developers build phone agents, voice assistants, and live translation tools that respond in under a second. The model has a 32K token context window and charges $5 per million input text tokens and $20 per million output text tokens, with separate, higher rates for audio tokens. It competes with Google’s Gemini Live API and various speech-focused startups building on top of Whisper-class transcription stacked with a language model, but its selling point is the single-model, low-latency architecture rather than a stitched-together pipeline.

item.title: GPT-5
item.description: GPT-5 is the model OpenAI released on August 7, 2025, folding its previous split between fast chat models (GPT-4o) and slow reasoning models (the o-series) into one system that decides on its own how much internal reasoning a given prompt needs. Rather than making users pick a model, ChatGPT and the API route each request to a lighter or heavier internal mode automatically, cutting the number of consumer-facing choices while still letting API customers set an explicit reasoning effort. It ships with a 400K token context window (272K input, 128K output), API pricing of $1.25 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, and scored around 90 on MMLU alongside strong marks on coding and agentic benchmarks at launch. OpenAI framed it as a jump in reliability and reduced hallucination rate rather than a dramatic leap in raw capability, positioning it against Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro and Anthropic’s Claude models of the same era. By mid-2026 OpenAI had already iterated past it with the GPT-5.x line, including the GPT-5.6 family, but GPT-5 remains available in the API and ChatGPT.

item.title: GPT-5.6 Luna
item.description: GPT-5.6 Luna is the fast, low-cost tier of OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 family, which began a limited government-vetted preview in late June 2026 before opening to the wider public on July 9, 2026 once the US Commerce Department’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation cleared broader access. Luna is built for summarization, drafting, and high-volume automation where speed and cost matter more than maximum reasoning depth, and it shares the family’s 1.05 million token context window with support for up to 128,000 output tokens. At $1 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens, it undercuts the mid-tier Terra model by a wide margin while still handling everyday chat and lightweight coding tasks. OpenAI pitched the three-tier Sol, Terra, Luna structure as a way for developers to trade off cost against capability without switching model families, following the same pattern it used with the GPT-5 mini and nano tiers.

item.title: GPT-5.6 Sol
item.description: GPT-5.6 Sol is OpenAI’s flagship model in the GPT-5.6 family, built for frontier reasoning, complex coding, multi-step agentic work, and cybersecurity research. OpenAI first shipped it as a locked-down preview to a small group of US-government-vetted organizations in late June 2026, then opened it to the public on July 9, 2026 after regulatory review cleared wider access. It carries the family’s 1.05 million token context window and 128,000 token output limit, priced at $5 per million input tokens and $30 per million output tokens, the highest tier of the three. OpenAI says Sol launched with its most extensive safety stack yet, adding tighter controls around sensitive cyber-related requests and repeated misuse attempts given its stronger offensive and defensive security capabilities. Rather than reporting the older MMLU-style academic scores, OpenAI emphasized agentic and practical benchmarks for this release, a shift several independent reviewers noted as a departure from prior GPT-5.x announcements.

item.title: GPT-5.6 Terra
item.description: GPT-5.6 Terra is the balanced, middle tier of OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 family, aimed at everyday coding, reasoning, and agentic tasks where Sol’s top-end capability would be overkill. It reached the public on July 9, 2026, following a preview period restricted to organizations vetted by the US government, and shares the family’s 1.05 million token context window and 128,000 token output cap. OpenAI prices it at $2.50 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, roughly half the cost of Sol, and describes its performance as competitive with the prior GPT-5.5 generation at that lower price. Terra is meant to be the default choice for developers who need strong reasoning and coding ability without paying flagship rates, similar to the role GPT-5’s mini tier played in the previous generation. It is available through ChatGPT, Azure OpenAI, and the standard API, and GitHub added it to Copilot the same day it launched.

item.title: GPT-Image-1
item.description: GPT-Image-1 is OpenAI’s native multimodal image generation model, the technology behind the image generator built into ChatGPT and offered separately through the Images API since April 23, 2025. Unlike the DALL-E series, which used a diffusion process, GPT-Image-1 generates images autoregressively within the same architecture family as OpenAI’s language models, which is why it follows detailed instructions and renders legible text inside images noticeably better than its predecessors. It supports text-to-image generation and editing at three quality tiers and three resolutions, including square, portrait, and landscape formats, with per-image pricing that scales from roughly a cent to about a quarter of a dollar depending on quality and size. It competes directly with Google’s Imagen and Midjourney for prompt-following and text rendering, and it has been widely adopted by developers building design and marketing tools on top of the API. OpenAI has already moved on to GPT-Image-1.5 and newer versions, and has set an October 23, 2026 deprecation date for the original GPT-Image-1 endpoint.

item.title: GPT-OSS-120B
item.description: GPT-OSS-120B is an open-weight reasoning model OpenAI released on August 5, 2025, marking its first open model release since GPT-2 in 2019. It uses a mixture-of-experts transformer architecture with 117 billion total parameters but only about 5.1 billion active per token, which lets it run reasoning-heavy workloads on a single high-end GPU instead of the multi-GPU clusters dense models of similar size would need. It scored around 90 on MMLU at launch, putting it in the same range as OpenAI’s own o4-mini on many reasoning and coding benchmarks, and it ships under the Apache 2.0 license so companies can self-host it, fine-tune it, and run it without usage restrictions. OpenAI built it specifically to compete with open releases from Meta, Mistral, and Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Alibaba’s Qwen team, which had been setting the pace in open-weight models while OpenAI stayed closed. It is available through Hugging Face, Together AI, Azure AI Foundry, and OpenAI’s own API for organizations that want the option of both open self-hosting and managed hosting.

item.title: GPT-OSS-20B
item.description: GPT-OSS-20B is the smaller of the two open-weight models OpenAI released on August 5, 2025, alongside the larger GPT-OSS-120B, in its first open model release since GPT-2. It uses a mixture-of-experts design with about 21 billion total parameters and roughly 3.6 billion active per token, light enough to run on a single consumer GPU with 16GB or more of memory, which was the point: OpenAI built it for developers and hobbyists who wanted a capable reasoning model without server-grade hardware. It scored 85.3 on MMLU at launch, a strong result for its size class, and handles coding, math, and general reasoning tasks reasonably close to its bigger sibling despite the much smaller footprint. Released under the Apache 2.0 license, it can be fine-tuned and redistributed freely, and it is available through Hugging Face, Together AI, and OpenAI’s API for teams that want a managed option instead of self-hosting.

item.title: Granite 13B
item.description: Granite 13B is one of IBM’s first foundation models built for its watsonx enterprise AI platform, announced on September 7, 2023 alongside a family of Granite models aimed at business use cases rather than general chat. It has 13 billion parameters, uses multi-query attention with learned position embeddings, and was trained with the tokenizer from EleutherAI’s GPT-NeoX-20B, giving it an 8,192 token context window. IBM built it for tasks like document summarization, question answering, and text classification inside regulated industries such as banking and insurance, and it came with IBM’s standard indemnification for customers worried about training-data copyright exposure, a selling point competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic did not offer at the time. Granite 13B was proprietary and accessible only through watsonx, distinguishing it from IBM’s later Granite 3 generation, which shifted toward openly licensed weights on Hugging Face. It has since been superseded by newer Granite versions as IBM’s enterprise AI lineup moved toward open weights and broader benchmark parity with mainstream models.

item.title: Grok 3
item.description: Grok 3 is xAI’s model released on February 17, 2025, trained on the Colossus supercomputer in Memphis using more than 200,000 GPUs, roughly ten times the compute xAI put into Grok-2. xAI pitched it as a reasoning model with a “Think” mode that can spend anywhere from seconds to minutes working through a problem, checking its own steps and backtracking before answering, and it reported an Elo score of 1402 on Chatbot Arena along with strong results on GPQA, AIME math competition problems, and MMLU-Pro. The context window grew to 1 million tokens, eight times what earlier Grok models supported, letting it handle much longer documents and codebases in one request. Grok 3 is priced at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens through xAI’s API, and it’s also available through the Grok app and X. xAI positioned it against OpenAI’s o3, Gemini 2 Pro, and DeepSeek V3, claiming an edge in math and science reasoning at launch.

item.title: Grok 4
item.description: Grok 4 is xAI’s flagship model released on July 9, 2025, positioned as a reasoning-first successor to Grok 3 with heavier test-time compute and a redesigned training pipeline. At launch, Artificial Analysis measured it at the top of its Intelligence Index, ahead of OpenAI’s o3 and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro at the time, and xAI reported an all-time-high GPQA Diamond score near 88 percent along with a joint-best AIME 2024 score around 94 percent. It supports a 256,000-token context window and handles both text and images, and xAI made it available through the Grok app, X, and the API at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. Grok 4’s launch drew attention beyond benchmarks too, including scrutiny over some of its unfiltered responses on X, which xAI addressed with follow-up moderation changes. It set the baseline that xAI’s later Grok 4 Fast and Grok 4.5 releases built on through 2025 and 2026.

item.title: Grok 4 Fast
item.description: Grok 4 Fast is xAI’s cost- and latency-optimized tier of Grok 4, released September 19, 2025 for high-volume use cases like customer support, search, and agentic tool calling where running the full Grok 4 model on every request would be too slow or expensive. Despite the “fast” branding, it keeps a large 2-million-token context window and ships in both reasoning and non-reasoning variants so developers can pick the latency profile they need. Pricing is aggressive at $0.20 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, undercutting most other frontier-adjacent models on a cost basis while still drawing on the same underlying Grok 4 training. xAI markets it heavily on agentic benchmarks and tool-use tasks rather than raw knowledge tests, and it’s available only through the API rather than the consumer Grok app or X.

item.title: Grok 4.5
item.description: Grok 4.5 is xAI’s model released on July 8, 2026, built with a heavier emphasis on coding, agentic workflows, and knowledge work than earlier Grok releases. On the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index it scored 54, placing fourth overall among frontier models while taking the top spot specifically on agentic tool use, and it posted 83.3 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 64.7 percent on SWE-Bench Pro, both benchmarks aimed at real coding and terminal tasks rather than multiple-choice knowledge tests. It carries a 1-million-token context window and handles text and image input, and xAI priced it at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens, with a cheaper $0.50 rate for cached input tokens. It’s reachable through the xAI API console, the Grok app, X, and a wide set of third-party integrations including Cursor, OpenRouter, Vercel, and Microsoft’s Word, Excel, and PowerPoint add-ins. Some coverage framed it as xAI’s answer to Anthropic’s Opus-class models, given the shared focus on long agentic coding sessions.

item.title: Grok-2
item.description: Grok-2 is xAI’s model released in beta on August 13, 2024, alongside a smaller Grok-2 mini variant. It was the first Grok model to reach a wide audience with both image understanding and native image generation, the latter built on a partnership with Black Forest Labs’ Flux model, and it integrates directly with X for access to real-time posts and trends. On released benchmarks, xAI reported an MMLU score around 87.5 percent along with strong results on GPQA, MATH, and document visual question answering, putting it roughly in line with GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro class models at the time. Grok-2 is available through X, the standalone Grok app, and xAI’s API at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. It remained xAI’s flagship offering until Grok 3 arrived in February 2025, and a later Grok-2 checkpoint (Grok-2-1212) continued to see API use even after that.

item.title: GTE-large
item.description: GTE-large is a text embedding model from Alibaba DAMO Academy, published on Hugging Face in mid-2023 as part of the General Text Embeddings (GTE) family alongside smaller GTE-base and GTE-small variants. It’s a 335-million-parameter BERT-style encoder trained with multi-stage contrastive learning on a broad mix of web and domain text, producing 1024-dimension vectors from inputs up to 512 tokens. The model is meant for retrieval, semantic search, clustering, and reranking, and at release it scored well on the MTEB benchmark leaderboard relative to other open embedding models of similar size, competing directly with BGE and E5 style models from other Chinese labs. GTE-large is open-weighted under Apache 2.0, runs easily on a single GPU or CPU for inference, and is distributed through Hugging Face and Alibaba Cloud, making it a common default choice for teams building RAG pipelines who want a compact embedding model without an API dependency.

item.title: Hunyuan DiT
item.description: Hunyuan-DiT is Tencent’s open-weight text-to-image model, built on a diffusion transformer architecture rather than the U-Net design most earlier diffusion models used. Tencent published it in May 2024, pairing a 1.5B-parameter denoising transformer with bilingual CLIP and multilingual T5 text encoders so it can follow prompts written in Chinese or English with similar fidelity. That bilingual focus is the model’s main selling point: most open text-to-image models of the time handled Chinese prompts poorly, and Hunyuan-DiT was trained specifically to close that gap. It generates 1024x1024 images and includes a built-in multimodal chat component that lets users refine an image across several turns of dialogue instead of rewriting the whole prompt each time. Tencent released the weights on Hugging Face and GitHub under its Hunyuan license, and later shipped a 1.1 update that fixed oversaturation and watermark artifacts present in the original checkpoint.

item.title: Hunyuan Turbo
item.description: Hunyuan Turbo is Tencent’s production-tier large language model, offered as an API-only service through Tencent Cloud rather than as open weights. Tencent positioned it as the fast, lower-cost counterpart to its larger flagship Hunyuan models, aimed at applications that need quick responses at scale, such as chat products and customer service bots built on WeChat and other Tencent platforms. The company has not disclosed the parameter count, consistent with how it handles its other proprietary API tiers, but has published pricing and periodically cut rates as it iterated toward successor tiers like Hunyuan Turbo S. It supports a 128K context window and is aimed at developers who want Hunyuan-family quality without paying for or waiting on the largest model in the lineup. Its main competition comes from other Chinese low-latency API tiers, including Alibaba’s Qwen-Turbo and Baidu’s ERNIE Speed.

item.title: Hunyuan3D
item.description: Hunyuan3D is Tencent’s open-weight system for turning text prompts or reference images into 3D assets, with the widely used 2.0 release published in January 2025. It splits the job into two models: a 2.6B-parameter shape generator built on a flow-based diffusion transformer that produces an untextured mesh, and a 1.3B-parameter texture model that paints high-resolution PBR materials onto that mesh afterward. That two-stage split lets each part specialize, so the shape model focuses purely on geometry while the texture model handles color, lighting response, and surface detail. Tencent released the weights on Hugging Face and GitHub under its Hunyuan license, giving game studios and 3D artists a way to run asset generation locally instead of through a paid API. It competes with other open and semi-open 3D generators such as TripoSR and Stability AI’s TripoSG, and later Hunyuan3D versions (2.1, 2.5) pushed texture fidelity and geometry detail further.

item.title: HyperCLOVA X
item.description: HyperCLOVA X is Naver’s flagship large language model, unveiled in August 2023 as South Korea’s answer to GPT-4 and one of the first major foundation models trained with a heavy emphasis on Korean language and cultural context rather than English-first data. Naver has said the model runs on roughly 204 billion parameters, more than GPT-3’s 175 billion, though the company has since focused on making later variants smaller and more efficient rather than simply larger. It powers Naver’s CLOVA X chat assistant and is available to businesses through Naver Cloud’s API, where it competes with global models on Korean-specific tasks like local search, e-commerce, and customer service where dialect, honorifics, and cultural references matter. Naver has followed the original release with specialized variants, including HyperCLOVA X Vision for image understanding and HyperCLOVA X THINK, a reasoning-focused version with an expanded context window. The strategy reflects a broader pattern of national or regional players building models tuned to a specific language market rather than competing head-on with OpenAI or Google on general capability alone.

item.title: HyperCLOVA X Vision
item.description: HyperCLOVA X Vision is Naver’s multimodal extension of its HyperCLOVA X language model, adding image understanding on top of the text model’s Korean-language strength. Naver introduced it in August 2024, and the company has said it answered 83.8 percent of Korean college entrance exam questions that included image inputs, ahead of the 77.8 percent Naver reported for GPT-4o on the same test. That benchmark matters for Naver’s pitch: rather than compete on generic multimodal leaderboards, the model is built to handle Korean-specific documents, exam questions, and visual context that Western models tend to get wrong. It’s available through Naver Cloud’s API and the CLOVA X app, aimed at Korean enterprises that need document QA, chart reading, or image-grounded chat in their own language. Naver has continued to expand the lineup with smaller open variants under the HyperCLOVA X SEED family and an omnimodal version that adds audio.

item.title: Ideogram 1.0
item.description: Ideogram 1.0 is the debut text-to-image model from Ideogram, a startup founded by ex-Google Brain researchers, released in February 2024 alongside an $80 million Series A round. Its standout feature at launch was legible in-image text: at the time, most diffusion models scrambled letters and words badly enough that adding readable text to a generated image was mostly a losing bet. Ideogram claimed roughly half the text-rendering error rate of competing models on its own evaluations, which made the model useful for things earlier tools struggled with, like posters, T-shirt designs, memes, and logos with real words in them. The model also shipped with Magic Prompt, a built-in prompt-expansion feature that fleshes out short user inputs into more detailed prompts before generation. Ideogram has since moved past 1.0 with 2.0 and 3.0 releases that pushed further on photorealism and typography, but 1.0 is the release that established text rendering as the company’s core differentiator against Midjourney and DALL-E.

item.title: Ideogram 2.0
item.description: Ideogram 2.0 is Ideogram’s second-generation text-to-image model, launched on August 21, 2024 and made free to all users on release day. It added five selectable style presets (regular, realistic, design, 3D, and anime), noticeably better rendering of hands, eyes, and skin in the realistic style, and color palette controls that let users lock a generation to specific brand or mood colors. The same launch introduced Ideogram Search, letting users browse over a billion public generations for inspiration, along with a new iOS app and a beta public API. Where Ideogram 1.0 was mainly known for solving legible in-image text, 2.0 broadened the pitch toward general image quality and stylistic control while keeping that typography advantage intact. It positioned Ideogram as a more complete competitor to Midjourney rather than a niche tool for text-heavy graphics alone.

item.title: Ideogram 3.0
item.description: Ideogram 3.0 is Ideogram’s third-generation image model, released on March 26, 2025 with sharper photorealism and a text-rendering accuracy that independent testing put around 90 percent, well ahead of the roughly 30 percent seen on Midjourney for similar short phrases. It introduced Style References, which let users upload a reference image and carry its visual style into new generations, plus Magic Fill and Extend, inpainting and outpainting tools built into Ideogram’s Canvas editor. Batch generation at scale is gated to paid plans, reflecting how Ideogram has increasingly split free and pro tiers by production-scale features rather than just image quality. API pricing lands around six cents per image, keeping it in a similar range to other commercial text-to-image APIs. The release keeps typography as Ideogram’s signature strength while catching up on editing tools that competitors like Midjourney and Adobe Firefly had already built out.

item.title: Imagen 2
item.description: Imagen 2 is Google DeepMind’s second-generation text-to-image model, previewed at Google I/O in May 2023 and made generally available on Vertex AI in December 2023. It improved photorealism and added logo and text rendering, an area where the original Imagen and most contemporaries were noticeably weak. Google positioned it as an enterprise-ready image model rather than a consumer toy, shipping it through Vertex AI with the customization tooling, managed infrastructure, and safety filtering that business customers expect from a cloud platform product. It later gained a short video-clip generation mode inside Vertex AI. Imagen 2 sat in Google’s lineup between the original Imagen research model and the more capable Imagen 3, which replaced it as Google’s primary image model through 2024.

item.title: Imagen 3
item.description: Imagen 3 is Google DeepMind’s third-generation text-to-image model, opened to Gemini and ImageFX users in August 2024. It improved on Imagen 2 in prompt understanding, image detail, and text rendering across multiple languages and scripts, and it supports five aspect ratios so users aren’t stuck with square output by default. Google rolled it out gradually, first to Gemini Advanced, Business, and Enterprise users before wider access, partly to phase in safeguards around generating images of real people. It’s available through Vertex AI for developers and through the Gemini app for consumers, putting it in direct competition with OpenAI’s DALL-E 3 and Midjourney on general-purpose image quality. Google later replaced it with Imagen 4 as its flagship image model, but Imagen 3 remained Google’s main text-to-image offering for roughly a year.

item.title: Imagen 4
item.description: Imagen 4 is Google DeepMind’s text-to-image model, announced at Google I/O in May 2025 and made generally available through the Gemini API and Vertex AI. It generates images at resolutions up to 2K and renders legible text and typography inside images, an area where earlier Imagen versions and many competing models struggled. Google ships it as a family of three variants: a fast tier built for quick drafts at roughly ten times the speed of Imagen 3, a standard tier, and an Ultra tier for maximum fidelity and prompt adherence. Pricing is per image and tiered by variant, with the fast option priced lowest and Ultra priced highest.

item.title: Jina Embeddings v2
item.description: Jina Embeddings v2 is a text embedding model from Jina AI, released in October 2023. It came in two main sizes, a 33 million parameter small version and a 137 million parameter base version, both built on a modified BERT architecture using ALiBi position encoding instead of standard positional embeddings. That choice let it handle sequences up to 8,192 tokens, which was unusual for an open embedding model at the time and let it compete with OpenAI’s proprietary text-embedding-ada-002 on long document retrieval while being far smaller. The model is released under an Apache 2.0 license and can be run locally or accessed through Jina’s API. It has since been superseded by jina-embeddings-v3, which adds multilingual support and task-specific adapters, but v2 remains in use for English-language retrieval tasks where its smaller size is an advantage.

item.title: Kimi K1.5
item.description: Kimi K1.5 is Moonshot AI’s first reasoning-focused model, released in January 2025 as the company’s answer to OpenAI’s o1. It is trained with reinforcement learning on long chains of thought and can reason jointly over text and images, which let Moonshot claim results on par with o1 on math, coding, and multimodal benchmarks like MathVista, AIME, and Codeforces. The model supports a 128,000-token context window and includes a “long2short” technique that transfers reasoning gains from long chains of thought into shorter, faster responses for everyday queries. Moonshot has not disclosed the parameter count. K1.5 was Moonshot’s proof that a Chinese lab could compete at the reasoning frontier, and it set the stage for the open-weight Kimi K2 line that followed a few months later.

item.title: Kimi-Audio
item.description: Kimi-Audio is an open-weight audio foundation model from Moonshot AI, with pretrained and instruction-tuned 7B checkpoints released in late April 2025. It handles speech recognition, audio understanding, and speech generation in a single model, so it can transcribe audio, answer questions about a sound clip, and produce spoken output rather than needing separate models stitched together. Moonshot released the model along with an evaluation toolkit, and the weights and code are on GitHub and Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license. It sits alongside Kimi-VL and the Kimi K-series text models in Moonshot’s push to open-source specialized components rather than keep every capability behind a closed API, and it gives developers a free, self-hostable alternative to commercial speech models like OpenAI’s Whisper and Google’s audio models.

item.title: Kling 2.0
item.description: Kling 2.0 is Kuaishou’s video generation model, launched in April 2025 at the company’s “Inspiration Comes True” event alongside a matching image model, Ketu 2.0. It takes text prompts or reference images and turns them into video, and Kuaishou focused the upgrade on smoother, more natural motion after earlier Kling versions drew criticism for stiff or jerky animation. The Master Edition adds a multimodal video editing feature that lets users add, remove, or replace elements in an existing generated clip by feeding in new text or images, rather than starting a generation over from scratch. Kuaishou positions Kling as a direct competitor to Runway, Pika, and Sora, and the 2.0 release was aimed at closing the gap on complex prompts, camera movement, and visual consistency across a shot. Kuaishou has continued iterating quickly since, with 2.1, 2.6, and 3.0 following within about a year.

item.title: Kolors
item.description: Kolors is Kuaishou’s open-weight text-to-image model, released in July 2024. It is a latent diffusion model with about 2.6 billion parameters, built on a U-Net architecture, and it uses ChatGLM as its text encoder instead of a CLIP-style encoder, which gives it a notable edge at reading and rendering Chinese-language prompts and Chinese text within images. It generates at a native 1024x1024 resolution and supports multiple aspect ratios. Kuaishou trained it on billions of text-image pairs and released the weights on GitHub and Hugging Face, free for research use, with a separate registration process required for commercial deployment. Alongside models like Flux and Stable Diffusion 3, Kolors is one of the few widely-used open image models that handles non-Latin scripts well.

item.title: Leonardo Diffusion XL
item.description: Leonardo Diffusion XL is one of Leonardo AI’s earlier in-house models, a fine-tune built on Stability AI’s Stable Diffusion XL architecture rather than a model trained from scratch. It was tuned to produce strong results from short, simple prompts, which made it a popular default for users who did not want to write long descriptive prompts to get usable output. It covers a broad range of styles, from photography to illustration, and became one of the more widely used models on the Leonardo platform before the company shipped its own foundational model, Phoenix, at the end of 2024. Leonardo AI, founded in Sydney in 2022, was acquired by Canva in July 2024, and Diffusion XL is now maintained mainly for users with existing workflows built around it rather than promoted as the platform’s leading option.

item.title: Leonardo Phoenix
item.description: Leonardo Phoenix is Leonardo AI’s first foundational image model trained in-house rather than fine-tuned from a third-party base, launched December 18, 2024 alongside Flux Dev and Flux Schnell support on the platform. Leonardo built it specifically to close the prompt-adherence gap with competitors: it follows long, detailed instructions closely and can render short strings of coherent text inside an image, a common weak spot for diffusion models of that era. It works across a wide range of styles at high fidelity and is available through both the Leonardo app and API, positioning it against models like Midjourney and DALL-E for creators who need precise control over output rather than loose interpretation of a prompt. Leonardo followed it with Phoenix 2.0 in late 2025, which added a consistent-character engine, faster generation, and basic image-to-video motion, building on the same foundation this original model established.

item.title: Llama 3.1 70B
item.description: Llama 3.1 70B is the middle tier of Meta’s July 2024 Llama 3.1 release, sitting between the 8 billion parameter version and the 405 billion parameter flagship. Meta trained the whole family on more than 15 trillion tokens and extended the context window to 128,000 tokens, a big jump from the 8,192 tokens of the original Llama 3. The 70B model added multilingual support and better tool use, and on benchmarks like MMLU and HumanEval it lands close to the far larger 405B model at a fraction of the compute cost. Because Meta released the weights openly under the Llama 3.1 Community License, the 70B tier became a common choice for companies that wanted strong quality they could self-host or run through third-party API providers such as Together AI and AWS Bedrock.

item.title: Luma Dream Machine 1.0
item.description: Luma Dream Machine 1.0 is Luma AI’s first publicly available video generation model, launched in June 2024 as a free web tool that turns text prompts or a starting image into short video clips. It generates roughly five-second shots and was notable at launch for handling physics and motion more convincingly than most competing video models at the time, keeping characters and objects consistent as they move rather than warping between frames. Luma built it as a large-scale generative transformer trained directly on video and text, distinct from the diffusion-based approaches several rivals used. The tool grew quickly after launch, reportedly passing 25 million registered users, and it made Luma one of the more visible names in AI video generation alongside Runway and Pika.

item.title: Luma Photon
item.description: Luma Photon is Luma AI’s image generation model, launched in November 2024 as a companion to its Dream Machine video tools. It is built on the same underlying multimodal architecture Luma uses for video, which the company says lets it render more consistent characters, scenes, and camera-like framing than typical diffusion-based image generators. Photon shipped alongside a faster, cheaper variant called Photon Flash, with API pricing around $0.015 per 1080p image for the full model and a fraction of that for Flash. Luma positioned Photon as a low-cost, high-throughput option for creative and marketing teams generating large volumes of images through its API or the Dream Machine app.

item.title: Luma Ray 3
item.description: Luma Ray 3 is Luma AI’s flagship video generation model, released in September 2025 as what the company calls the first reasoning video model. Rather than generating pixels directly from a prompt, Ray 3 produces both text and visual tokens as it works, planning a scene and checking its own output before finalizing a clip, similar to a director sketching a storyboard before shooting. It is also the first video model to output true 10, 12, and 16-bit HDR footage in ACES2065-1 EXR format, aimed at professional film and advertising pipelines rather than just social clips. A Draft Mode lets users generate many quick low-cost variations before committing to a final high-resolution HDR render, and Adobe added Ray 3 to Firefly shortly after launch, giving it a route into mainstream creative software.

item.title: Luminous
item.description: Luminous is a family of large language models from the German company Aleph Alpha, first released in April 2022 in three sizes: Luminous Base, Extended, and Supreme, with the largest Supreme tier reaching 70 billion parameters by that August. Aleph Alpha built Luminous as a multilingual model with an early focus on European languages and enterprise use cases where regulatory compliance and data residency in the EU matter. Its most distinctive feature is explainability: Luminous can point back to the specific passages in its input that a given output was based on, a source-attribution capability aimed at industries like law, finance, and government that need to audit AI-generated answers. Aleph Alpha positions Luminous as a European alternative to US-based models from OpenAI and Google, sold mainly to enterprise and public-sector customers through its own API rather than to general consumers.

item.title: Lyria
item.description: Lyria is Google DeepMind’s music generation model, built to turn text prompts into produced audio tracks. The version available through Vertex AI (Lyria 2) generates instrumental music from text descriptions, handling a wide range of genres and picking up on the texture of individual instruments, while the streaming variant, Lyria RealTime, produces continuous music over a WebSocket connection that responds to live parameter changes. DeepMind pairs every clip with a SynthID watermark so the audio can be identified as AI-generated after the fact.

item.title: Mistral Embed
item.description:
Mistral Embed is Mistral AI’s text embedding model, available through its API since early 2024, that converts text into 1024-dimensional vectors for semantic search, clustering, and retrieval-augmented generation. It accepts inputs up to 8,192 tokens and Mistral positions it as a general-purpose embedding option for teams already building on the Mistral platform, rather than a specialized model for code or multilingual retrieval.

It is priced at $0.01 per million input tokens, making it one of the cheaper hosted embedding options available, and is accessed exclusively through Mistral’s API rather than as downloadable weights. Mistral later added Codestral Embed, a separate model tuned specifically for code retrieval, leaving Mistral Embed as the general-text option in its lineup.

item.title: Mistral Large 2
item.description: Mistral Large 2 is a 123 billion parameter dense language model that Mistral AI released on July 24, 2024, replacing the original Mistral Large as the company’s flagship offering. It handles a 128,000-token context window, scores 84.0% on MMLU, and Mistral trained it with heavy emphasis on multilingual ability, covering languages including French, German, Spanish, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, and Hindi alongside English, plus more than 80 programming languages for code generation.

item.title: Mistral Large 3
item.description: Mistral Large 3 is Mistral AI’s flagship language model, released on December 2, 2025 as part of the broader Mistral 3 lineup. It uses a sparse mixture-of-experts design with 675 billion total parameters but only about 41 billion active per token, so it runs at roughly the compute cost of a much smaller dense model while drawing on a far larger pool of learned weights. It takes both text and images as input, handles a 256,000-token context window, and Mistral released the weights under an Apache 2.0 license, a departure from the closed approach it took with Mistral Large 2.

item.title: AgentOps
item.description: AgentOps addresses a problem specific to AI agents: they make many decisions, call tools, and chain model requests, which makes failures hard to understand. By adding a few lines of code, developers record each agent session, and the platform shows a timeline of prompts, model responses, tool calls, and errors. A replay view lets you walk through exactly what the agent did, which helps find why it looped, hallucinated, or failed to finish.

item.title: Anyscale
item.description: Anyscale was founded by the creators of Ray, a framework that makes it easier to spread Python code across many machines. Ray is widely used in AI for tasks such as distributed model training, large-scale data processing, reinforcement learning, and serving models, and it is the engine behind a number of big AI systems. Anyscale offers a managed platform that handles cluster setup, scaling, and monitoring, so teams do not have to operate the infrastructure themselves.

item.title: Baseten
item.description:
Baseten runs models for companies that build AI products. A team packages a model, often with the Truss open-source tool, and deploys it as an endpoint that scales up and down with demand. The platform handles GPU provisioning, scaling, and monitoring, which are chores that distract from building the product.

It focuses on performance. Optimized inference engines, quick cold starts, and support for the latest GPUs help serve models with low latency and cost. Teams can deploy open models from a library, bring their own, or fine-tune, and use dedicated deployments for steady traffic. Options for running in a customer’s own cloud address security needs.

item.title: BentoML
item.description:
BentoML tackles the step between a working model and a running service. A developer writes a small Python service that loads a model, defines an API, and handles requests. BentoML builds this into a standard package, called a Bento, that includes dependencies and can be turned into a Docker container.

The framework supports features that production services need: batching requests for efficiency, running multiple models, GPU use, and monitoring. It works with models from PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn, Hugging Face, and others, and supports large language model serving through optimized backends. BentoCloud is the company’s managed platform for deploying and scaling.

item.title: DataStax
item.description:
DataStax grew up around Apache Cassandra, a database designed for large, always-on applications. Its Astra DB service runs Cassandra in the cloud without servers to manage, and adds vector search so developers can store embeddings and find similar items by meaning. That makes it a base for retrieval-augmented generation, recommendations, and chat features.

The company also supports the tools around AI development. Langflow is a visual builder for agent and retrieval workflows, and its data APIs let developers use document or table models. Pairing a scalable database with AI tools gives teams a path from prototype to large production workloads.

item.title: DeepInfra
item.description:
DeepInfra hosts open models and sells access by the token or by usage. A developer picks a model from its catalog, which includes chat models, embeddings, image generators, and speech tools, and calls it with an API compatible with OpenAI’s format. The company handles GPUs, scaling, and optimization.

The appeal is price and simplicity. Because open models are widely available, hosting providers compete on cost and speed, and DeepInfra positions itself at the low end. Developers can also deploy custom models or fine-tuned versions in some cases, and use dedicated GPUs for steady workloads.

item.title: Eden AI
item.description:
Eden AI addresses the problem of integrating many AI vendors. Each provider has its own API, formats, and billing. Eden AI offers one API for tasks like text generation, translation, OCR, speech recognition, image analysis, and more, and routes the request to the provider a developer chooses.

That makes comparison simple: the same input can be sent to several providers to see which gives the best result for the price. Fallback options switch to another provider if one fails, and a single bill and dashboard track usage. Workflows allow chaining several AI steps.

item.title: Firecrawl
item.description:
Firecrawl solves a common step in AI projects: getting web content into a form language models can use. A developer gives it a URL, and it fetches the page, handles JavaScript rendering, removes boilerplate, and returns clean Markdown. It can also crawl a whole site, map its links, or extract structured fields from pages using a schema.

Search and agent features expand its use. Developers can search the web and scrape results in one call, or use an endpoint that gathers data across many pages from a plain description. Integrations connect to frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex and to tools via the Model Context Protocol. The core is open source and can be self-hosted.

item.title: Haystack
item.description:
Haystack helps developers assemble applications that answer questions over documents. A pipeline strings together components: converting files, splitting text, creating embeddings, retrieving relevant passages, and generating an answer with a language model. Each component is swappable, so teams can change a model or database without rewriting everything.

The framework supports many model providers and vector stores, hybrid search, evaluation tools, and agents that use tools. It also provides a way to serialize pipelines, which supports deployment and testing. deepset offers a commercial platform around it for companies that want managed hosting and collaboration.

item.title: MLflow
item.description:
MLflow began at Databricks as a way to bring order to machine learning work. Teams log parameters, metrics, code versions, and artifacts for each run, compare results in a web interface, and package models in a standard format that can be deployed in many environments. A model registry manages versions and stages.

The project has extended to generative AI. It supports tracing of LLM applications, evaluation tools, and prompt management, making it useful for teams building with language models as well as classic models. It works with most ML libraries and cloud platforms.

item.title: Promptfoo
item.description:
Promptfoo helps developers test AI systems systematically. A user defines test cases and criteria in a configuration file, runs prompts across models, and compares outputs side by side, with assertions that check for expected content, format, or safety. It runs from the command line and in CI pipelines.

Red-teaming features generate adversarial inputs to probe for jailbreaks, prompt injection, data leaks, and other vulnerabilities, and report where an application fails. It supports many providers and local models and has been widely adopted.

item.title: Ragas
item.description:
Ragas helps teams measure how well a RAG system works. A developer feeds in questions, retrieved passages, and generated answers, and Ragas uses language models to score aspects like whether the answer is supported by the context, whether it addresses the question, and whether the retrieved context was relevant.

Because it does not require hand-labeled answers for every case, teams can evaluate quickly, and it can generate synthetic test sets from documents. It integrates with frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex and with observability tools.

item.title: Render
item.description:
Render simplifies hosting. A developer connects a repository, and Render builds and runs the app, handles TLS certificates, and scales as needed. It supports web services, static sites, cron jobs, private services, and managed Postgres and Redis.

Preview environments build each pull request automatically, and infrastructure can be defined in a file. Teams like its predictable pricing and straightforward interface, and it works for AI apps that need background workers and databases.

item.title: SambaNova
item.description:
SambaNova designs custom chips, called reconfigurable dataflow units, along with the software and systems around them. The goal is high-speed inference and training for large language models at lower power than general-purpose GPU setups.

Its cloud service offers fast access to open models through an API, and enterprises can deploy systems on premises for data control. Government and large organizations are among its customers.

SambaNova is sold on usage-based cloud pricing and system contracts. The company has faced a competitive field of chip makers and has been the subject of reports about funding and acquisition talks, so check its status. Alternatives include Groq, Cerebras, NVIDIA, Together AI, and Fireworks AI. SambaNova suits organizations needing fast inference.

item.title: ScrapeGraph AI
